chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — London. A Room in the palace
paragraphs: [King Richard, John of Gaunt, other noblemen and attendants enter.]

KING RICHARD. Old John of Gaunt, honored Duke of Lancaster, have you kept your solemn promise? Have you brought your bold son, Henry Hereford, here? He must now back up the violent accusation he recently made against the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray. At the time I had no free moment to hear it.
GAUNT. I have, my lord.

KING RICHARD. Tell me, too, have you tested him on this? Does he accuse the Duke out of some old grudge? Or does he do it rightly, as a good subject should, because he knows of real treachery in the man?
GAUNT. As far as I could get to the bottom of it, he does it because he saw some clear danger in Mowbray aimed at Your Highness. It isn’t a long-standing grudge.

KING RICHARD. Then call them in to me. I will hear the accuser and the accused speak freely, face to face, glaring at each other brow to brow. They are both proud and full of fury. In their rage they are as deaf as the sea and as rash as fire.
[Bolingbroke and Mowbray enter.]
BOLINGBROKE. May many years of happy days come to my gracious king, my most loving lord!
MOWBRAY. May each day outdo the happiness of the one before, until heaven, jealous of earth’s good luck, adds an immortal title to your crown!

KING RICHARD. I thank you both. But one of you is only flattering me, as the reason you came here makes plain: you have come to accuse each other of high treason. Cousin Hereford, what is your charge against the Duke of Norfolk, Thomas Mowbray?

BOLINGBROKE. First—and may heaven witness what I say!—I come before my prince as his accuser out of a subject’s loving devotion. I care for my prince’s precious safety, and I am free of any other, wrongly born hatred. Now, Thomas Mowbray, I turn to you, and listen closely to my greeting. What I say my body will prove here on earth, or my immortal soul will answer for it in heaven. You are a traitor and a villain. You are too well-born to be one and too wicked to live. The clearer and brighter the sky is, the uglier the clouds that fly across it look. And to make the charge worse, I’ll say it again: I stuff the name of foul traitor down your throat. Before I leave this spot, I hope, if my king allows it, that my sword, drawn in a just cause, will prove what my tongue says.

MOWBRAY. Don’t let my calm words here make you doubt how strongly I feel. This dispute between the two of us can’t be settled by a women’s war of words, by two eager tongues shouting bitterly at each other. Hot blood must be cooled, by spilling it, to decide this. Still, I can’t claim to be so tamely patient that I keep quiet and say nothing at all. First, my respect for Your Highness holds me back. It keeps me from giving rein and spur to my speech. Otherwise my words would gallop on until they had driven these charges of treason back down his throat twice over. Put aside his royal blood, and pretend he is no relative of my king. Then I defy him and I spit at him. I call him a slandering coward and a villain. To prove it I would give him an advantage. I would meet him even if I had to run there on foot, to the frozen ridges of the Alps. Or I would meet him on any other ground where no one can live, wherever an Englishman ever dared to set foot. In the meantime let this defend my loyalty: by everything I hope for, he lies, and lies utterly.

BOLINGBROKE. Pale, trembling coward, there I throw down my glove as a challenge. Here I give up my kinship with the King and set aside my royal blood. It’s your fear, not your respect, that makes you use that as an excuse. If guilty terror has left you strength enough to pick up the pledge of my honor, then bend down and take it. By that pledge and by every other rite of knighthood, I will prove against you in single combat what I have said, or anything worse you can think up.

MOWBRAY. I pick it up. And I swear by the sword that gently touched my shoulder when I was knighted: I will answer you in any fair way, by any rule of knightly trial. Once I mount my horse, may I never get down alive if I am a traitor or fight unjustly!
KING RICHARD. What does my cousin accuse Mowbray of? It must be something great to make me even think ill of him.

BOLINGBROKE. Whatever I say, my life will prove true. Mowbray received eight thousand gold coins as advance pay for Your Highness’s soldiers. He kept them for wicked purposes, like a false traitor and a harmful villain. Besides that, I say, and will prove in battle, here or anywhere else, to the farthest edge ever seen by English eyes, that every treason plotted and schemed in this land for the past eighteen years comes from false Mowbray as its source and spring. I say more, and will prove all this on his wicked life. He plotted the death of the Duke of Gloucester. He egged on Gloucester’s enemies, who were quick to believe him. And so, like a cowardly traitor, he drained out the Duke’s innocent soul in streams of blood. That blood, like the blood of Abel the sacrificer, cries out to me even from the tongueless caves of the earth for justice and harsh punishment. And by the glorious worth of my ancestry, this arm will deliver it, or I will die trying.
KING RICHARD. How high his determination soars, like a falcon! Thomas of Norfolk, what do you say to this?
MOWBRAY. Oh, let my king turn his face away and make his ears deaf for a little while. Let me tell this disgrace to his royal blood how much God and good men hate such a filthy liar.

KING RICHARD. Mowbray, my eyes and ears are impartial. He is only my father’s brother’s son. But even if he were my brother, no, even my heir, I make this vow by the power of my scepter. Being so close to my sacred blood would give him no privilege. It would not bend the firm, upright judgment of my soul. He is my subject, Mowbray, and so are you. I allow you to speak freely and without fear.

MOWBRAY. Then, Bolingbroke, you lie, from your lying throat all the way down to your heart. Three-quarters of the money I received for the Calais garrison I duly paid out to His Highness’s soldiers. I kept the rest with his consent. My king owed me that money as the balance of a large debt from my last trip to France, when I went to bring back his queen. So swallow that lie. As for Gloucester’s death, I did not kill him. But to my own shame I neglected my sworn duty in that matter. As for you, my noble Lord of Lancaster, the honorable father of my enemy: I once set an ambush to kill you. That crime troubles my grieving soul. But before I last took communion, I confessed it and begged Your Grace’s pardon in full, and I hope I received it. That is my fault. All the other charges come from the spite of a villain, a coward and a most debased traitor. I will boldly defend myself against them. In return I throw down my glove at this arrogant traitor’s foot. I will prove myself a loyal gentleman by spilling the best blood in his chest. To get that done quickly, I sincerely beg Your Highness to set the day of our trial.

KING RICHARD. Gentlemen, you are inflamed with anger; do as I say. Let’s purge this bad temper without bloodletting. This is my prescription, though I am no doctor: deep hatred cuts too deep a wound. Forget, forgive, settle it and agree. Our doctors say this is not the month for bleeding. Good uncle, let’s end this where it began. I’ll calm the Duke of Norfolk; you calm your son.
GAUNT. Making peace suits a man my age. My son, throw down the Duke of Norfolk’s glove.
KING RICHARD. And Norfolk, you throw down his.
GAUNT. Well, Harry, when? When will you do it? As your father I shouldn’t have to tell you twice.
KING RICHARD. Norfolk, throw it down; I command it. It’s no use refusing.

MOWBRAY. Dread king, I throw myself at your feet. You can command my life, but not my shame. My life I owe you as my duty. But my good name will live on my grave in spite of death, and you will not have it to use for dark dishonor. I am disgraced, accused and humiliated here. I am pierced to the soul by the poisoned spear of slander. Nothing can cure it but the heart’s blood of the man who breathed this poison.
KING RICHARD. Rage must be resisted. Give me his glove. Lions tame leopards.

MOWBRAY. Yes, but they can’t change the leopard’s spots. Take away my shame, and I’ll give up the glove. My dear, dear lord, the purest treasure in this mortal life is a spotless reputation. Without that, men are just gilded dirt or painted clay. A bold spirit in a loyal heart is like a jewel in a chest locked ten times over. My honor is my life; the two grow as one. Take my honor from me, and my life is over. So, my dear lord, let me put my honor to the test. I live by it, and I will die for it.
KING RICHARD. Cousin, give up his glove. You go first.

BOLINGBROKE. Oh, God keep my soul from such a deep sin! Shall I look beaten in front of my father? Shall I lower my rank with a beggar’s pale fear in front of this cowardly villain, who is already outfaced? Before my tongue wounds my honor with such a weak wrong, or sounds such a shameful call for a truce, my teeth will tear out that cowardly tongue, the servant of retreating fear. I’ll spit it out, bleeding, in deep disgrace, right into Mowbray’s face, where shame lives.
[Gaunt exits.]

KING RICHARD. I was not born to plead but to command. Since I can’t command you to be friends, be ready at Coventry on Saint Lambert’s Day, or answer for it with your lives. There your swords and lances will settle the swelling quarrel of your fixed hatred. Since I can’t reconcile you, we’ll watch justice declare which knight wins. Lord Marshal, order my officers-at-arms to be ready to manage this domestic fight.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — The same. A room in the Duke of Lancaster’s palace
paragraphs: [John of Gaunt enters with the Duchess of Gloucester.]

GAUNT. Alas, my own share in Woodstock’s blood urges me more than your cries do to act against the butchers who killed him. But the power to punish lies in the very hands that committed the crime we can’t punish. So let’s leave our quarrel to the will of heaven. When the heavens see the time is ripe on earth, they will rain burning vengeance on the heads of the guilty.

DUCHESS. Doesn’t brotherhood spur you on any harder than that? Has love no living fire left in your old blood? Edward’s seven sons, and you are one of them, were like seven vials of his sacred blood. They were like seven fine branches growing from one root. Some of those seven have dried up in the course of nature. Some of those branches have been cut by the Fates. But Thomas, my dear lord, my life, my Gloucester, was one vial full of Edward’s sacred blood. He was one flourishing branch of his most royal root. Now that vial is cracked and all the precious liquid spilled. That branch is hacked down and its summer leaves all withered, by the hand of envy and the bloody axe of murder. Ah, Gaunt! His blood was yours! The same bed, the same womb, the same metal, the same mold that formed you made him a man. Though you are alive and breathing, you were killed in him. You agree to your own father’s death, in large part, when you watch your poor brother die, for he was the image of your father’s life. Don’t call it patience, Gaunt; it’s despair. By letting your brother be slaughtered like this, you show the open road to your own life. You teach cruel murder how to butcher you. What we call patience in common men is pale, cold cowardice in noble hearts. What more can I say? The best way to protect your own life is to avenge my Gloucester’s death.

GAUNT. The quarrel belongs to God. God’s substitute, His deputy anointed in His sight, caused this death. If it was wrong, let heaven take revenge, for I can never raise an angry arm against God’s minister.
DUCHESS. Then where, alas, can I take my complaint?
GAUNT. To God, the champion and defender of widows.

DUCHESS. Well then, I will. Farewell, old Gaunt. You are going to Coventry to watch our cousin Hereford fight cruel Mowbray. Oh, may my husband’s wrongs ride on Hereford’s spear, so that it pierces butcher Mowbray’s chest! Or if bad luck makes him miss on the first charge, may Mowbray’s sins weigh so heavily in his chest that they break his foaming horse’s back. May they throw the rider headfirst into the lists, a cowardly wretch at the mercy of my cousin Hereford! Farewell, old Gaunt. Your brother’s wife, as I once was, must end her life with her only companion, Grief.
GAUNT. Sister, farewell. I must go to Coventry. May as much good stay with you as goes with me!

DUCHESS. Just one more word. Grief bounces where it falls, not because it is hollow and empty but because it is heavy. I’m saying goodbye before I’ve even begun, because sorrow doesn’t end when it seems to be finished. Give my regards to your brother, Edmund York. There, that’s all. No, don’t leave yet! Even if that’s all, don’t go so quickly. I’ll think of more. Tell him—ah, what?—to visit me at Plashy as soon as he can. Alas, and what will good old York see there? Only empty rooms and bare walls, servants’ quarters with no servants, and stone floors no one walks on. And what welcome will he hear there but my groans? So give him my regards, but don’t let him come there to look for sorrow, which lives everywhere. Desolate, desolate, I will go home and die! My weeping eye takes its last leave of you.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — Open Space, near Coventry. Lists set out, and a Throne. Heralds, &c., attending
paragraphs: [The Lord Marshal and the Duke of Aumerle enter.]
MARSHAL. My Lord Aumerle, is Harry Hereford armed?
AUMERLE. Yes, completely, and he can’t wait to enter.
MARSHAL. The Duke of Norfolk, lively and bold, is only waiting for the trumpet call from the accuser’s side.
AUMERLE. Then the champions are ready and are waiting only for His Majesty to arrive.

[King Richard enters and takes his seat on his throne. Gaunt, Bushy, Bagot, Green and others enter and take their places. A trumpet sounds and another trumpet answers from offstage. Then Mowbray, the defendant, enters in armor, led by a herald.]
KING RICHARD. Marshal, ask that champion over there why he has come here armed. Ask him his name, and then, following the proper order, have him swear that his cause is just.

MARSHAL. In the name of God and the King, tell me who you are. Tell me why you come here dressed in a knight’s armor, which man you have come to fight, and what your quarrel is. Speak truthfully, on your knighthood and your oath. If you do, may heaven and your courage defend you.

MOWBRAY. My name is Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk. I come here bound by my oath, and God forbid a knight should break one! I come both to defend my loyalty and truth to God, my king and my descendants against the Duke of Hereford, who accuses me. And by the grace of God and the strength of my arm, I come to prove, while defending myself, that he is a traitor to my God, my king and me. As I fight truly, may heaven defend me.
[He takes his seat.]
[A trumpet sounds. Bolingbroke, the accuser, enters in armor, led by a herald.]
KING RICHARD. Marshal, ask that armed knight over there who he is and why he comes here, covered in the plate armor of war. And in the proper legal form, have him swear to the justice of his cause.

MARSHAL. What is your name? And why do you come here before King Richard into his royal lists? Whom have you come to fight, and what is your quarrel? Speak like a true knight, and may heaven defend you!

BOLINGBROKE. I am Harry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby. I stand here ready in arms to prove in these lists, by God’s grace and my body’s courage, that Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, is a foul and dangerous traitor. He is a traitor to the God of heaven, to King Richard and to me. As I fight truly, may heaven defend me.
MARSHAL. On pain of death, let no one be so bold or reckless as to touch the barriers of the lists. Only the Marshal and the officers appointed to run this honorable contest may do so.

BOLINGBROKE. Lord Marshal, let me kiss my king’s hand and kneel before His Majesty. Mowbray and I are like two men who swear to go on a long, tiring pilgrimage. So let us take a formal leave and say a loving goodbye to our friends on each side.
MARSHAL. The accuser greets Your Highness with all due respect. He asks to kiss your hand and say goodbye.

KING RICHARD. [He comes down from his throne.] I will come down and take him in my arms. Cousin Hereford, as your cause is just, may your luck be just as good in this royal fight. Farewell, my own blood. If you shed your blood today, I may mourn you, but I may not avenge your death.

BOLINGBROKE. Oh, let no noble eye waste a tear on me if Mowbray’s spear gores me. I fight Mowbray as confidently as a falcon flies at a bird. My loving lord, I take my leave of you. And of you, my noble cousin, Lord Aumerle. I’m not sick, even though I have business with death. I’m lusty, young and breathing cheerfully. Look! As at English feasts, I greet the finest dish last, to make the end the sweetest. Oh you, the earthly source of my blood, your youthful spirit is reborn in me. It lifts me up with double strength to reach for the victory above my head. Make my armor stronger with your prayers. Harden my lance’s point with your blessings, so it may pierce Mowbray’s coat of armor as if it were wax. Let it polish up the name of John of Gaunt anew, through the vigorous conduct of his son.

GAUNT. May God make you succeed in your good cause. Be as swift as lightning in action. Let your blows, doubled and doubled again, fall like stunning thunder on the helmet of your hostile, deadly enemy. Stir up your young blood, be brave, and live.
BOLINGBROKE. May my innocence and Saint George help me win!
[He takes his seat.]

MOWBRAY. [Rising.] However God or fortune decides my fate, the man who lives or dies here is a loyal, just and honest gentleman, true to King Richard’s throne. No prisoner ever threw off his chains and embraced his golden, unlimited freedom with a happier heart than my dancing soul now celebrates this feast of battle with my enemy. My mighty king, and my fellow lords, accept my wish that you all have happy years. I go to fight as calmly and cheerfully as if I were going to a game. A man who is in the right has a peaceful heart.
KING RICHARD. Farewell, my lord. I can clearly see courage and virtue lying in your eye. Marshal, arrange the combat and begin.
[The King and the lords go back to their seats.]
MARSHAL. Harry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby, take your lance, and may God defend the side that is right.
BOLINGBROKE. [Rising.] My hope is as strong as a tower, and I say “Amen”!
MARSHAL. [To an officer.] Take this lance to Thomas, Duke of Norfolk.

FIRST HERALD. Here stands Harry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby, for God, for his king and for himself. On penalty of being declared a liar and a coward, he will prove that Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, is a traitor to his God, his king and to him. He dares Mowbray to come forward and fight.

SECOND HERALD. Here stands Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk, on penalty of being declared a liar and a coward. He is here both to defend himself and to prove that Henry of Hereford, Lancaster and Derby is disloyal to God, to his king and to him. He comes bravely and eagerly, and waits only for the signal to begin.
MARSHAL. Sound the trumpets. Combatants, advance.
[A trumpet sounds the charge.]
Stop! The King has thrown down his staff.

KING RICHARD. Tell them to put aside their helmets and their spears, and both go back to their chairs. Come away with me and my council, and let the trumpets play until we return and tell these dukes our decision.
[A long fanfare of trumpets.]

[To the combatants.] Come closer, and listen to what my council and I have decided. We do not want our kingdom’s soil stained with the precious blood it has raised. Our eyes hate the terrible sight of civil wounds dug open by neighbors’ swords. We think the soaring, eagle-winged pride of your ambitious thoughts, along with your envy of each other, drove you to disturb our peace. That peace lies in our country’s cradle like a baby breathing the sweet breath of gentle sleep. If it were woken by the noise of wild, tuneless drums, the dreadful bray of harsh trumpets and the grating crash of angry iron weapons, fair peace might be frightened out of our quiet borders. Then we would have to wade through the blood of our own relatives. For these reasons, we banish you both from our lands. You, cousin Hereford, on pain of death, shall not see our fair kingdom again until ten summers have ripened our fields. Instead you will walk the foreign roads of exile.

BOLINGBROKE. Your will be done. This will have to be my comfort: the same sun that warms you here will shine on me. The golden beams it lends to you here will fall on me too and make my exile glow like gold.

KING RICHARD. Norfolk, a heavier sentence waits for you, and I announce it somewhat unwillingly. The slow, creeping hours will never put an end to your bitter exile, because it has no end date. I pronounce against you the hopeless words “never to return,” on pain of death.

MOWBRAY. That is a heavy sentence, my most sovereign lord, and one I never expected to hear from your mouth. I deserved a better reward from your highness, not such a deep wound as being thrown out into the wide world. For forty years I have spoken my native English, and now I must give it up. From now on my tongue is no more use to me than a viol or harp with no strings. It is like a fine instrument shut in its case. Or, if the case is opened, it is put into the hands of someone who has no idea how to play it. You have jailed my tongue inside my mouth, locked twice behind the gates of my teeth and lips. Dull, numb, empty ignorance has been made my jailer, to watch over me. I am too old to cuddle up to a nurse, and too far along in years to start school now. So what is your sentence but a silent death, since it robs my tongue of the chance to speak its native language?
KING RICHARD. It does you no good to plead for pity. Complaining comes too late after we have given our sentence.
MOWBRAY. Then I turn away from the light of my country, to live in the gloomy shadows of endless night.
[He starts to leave.]

KING RICHARD. Come back, and take an oath before you go. Lay your banished hands on our royal sword. Swear by the duty you owe to God—we banish the duty you owe to us along with you—that you will keep the oath we now give you. Swear, so help you truth and God, that you will never be friends with each other in exile. Swear that you will never look at each other’s faces. Swear that you will never write to each other, greet each other, or patch up this dark storm of hatred that started at home. And swear that you will never deliberately meet to plot, scheme or conspire any harm against us, our government, our subjects or our country.
BOLINGBROKE. I swear.
MOWBRAY. And I swear to keep all of this too.

BOLINGBROKE. Norfolk, I say this much to you as my enemy. If the King had let us fight, by now one of our souls would be drifting in the air. It would be banished from the fragile tomb of its body, just as our bodies are now banished from this land. Confess your treasons before you leave the kingdom. You have a long way to go, so do not carry the heavy weight of a guilty soul along with you.

MOWBRAY. No, Bolingbroke. If I was ever a traitor, let my name be erased from the book of life, and let me be banished from heaven as I am banished from here! But God, you and I all know what you are. And I fear the King will regret it all too soon. Farewell, my lord. Now I cannot lose my way. Except for the road back to England, the whole world is my road.
[He exits.]

KING RICHARD. Uncle, I can see your grieving heart in the mirrors of your eyes. Your sad face has taken four years off his exile. [To Bolingbroke.] When six freezing winters are over, come home from exile, and you will be welcome.
BOLINGBROKE. What a long time fits inside one little word! Four dragging winters and four lively springs are ended with a word. That is the power of a king’s breath.

GAUNT. I thank you, my lord, for cutting four years from my son’s exile out of respect for me. But I will gain little from it. Before the six years he has left can pass through their months and seasons, my lamp will have run out of oil. My light, worn out by time, will be put out by old age and endless night. My little stub of candle will be burned down and finished, and blind death will not let me see my son.
KING RICHARD. Come now, uncle, you have many years left to live.

GAUNT. But you cannot give me a single minute of them, King. You can shorten my days with gloomy sorrow, and steal nights from me, but you cannot lend me one tomorrow. You can help time carve wrinkles into me with age, but you cannot stop a single wrinkle on its way. Time will accept your word as payment for my death. But once I am dead, your whole kingdom cannot buy back my breath.
KING RICHARD. Your son was banished on good advice, and your own voice was part of that verdict. So why do you seem to scowl at our justice?

GAUNT. Things that taste sweet often turn sour when you digest them. You asked me to speak as a judge, but I would have preferred you to let me argue like a father. Oh, if it had been a stranger and not my child, I would have been gentler and tried to excuse his fault. I wanted to avoid being accused of favoring my own son, and with that sentence I destroyed my own life. I kept waiting for one of you to say I was being too harsh in sending away my own son. But you let my unwilling tongue do me this wrong against my will.
KING RICHARD. Cousin, farewell. And uncle, tell him goodbye. We banish him for six years, and he must go.
[Trumpets sound. King Richard and his followers exit.]
AUMERLE. Cousin, farewell. Whatever you cannot tell us in person, let your letters tell us from wherever you are.
MARSHAL. My lord, I will not say goodbye yet, because I will ride beside you as far as the land goes.
GAUNT. Oh, why are you hoarding your words and not answering your friends’ goodbyes?
BOLINGBROKE. I have too few words to say goodbye to you properly. At a time like this my tongue ought to pour out words freely to express the overflowing sorrow in my heart.
GAUNT. Your grief is only that you will be away for a while.
BOLINGBROKE. When joy is absent, grief is present for that whole time.
GAUNT. What are six winters? They go by quickly.
BOLINGBROKE. They do for happy men. But grief makes one hour feel like ten.
GAUNT. Call it a trip you are taking for pleasure.
BOLINGBROKE. My heart will sigh if I call it by the wrong name, because it knows this is a forced pilgrimage.
GAUNT. Think of the gloomy journey of your tired steps as the setting that will make the precious jewel of your homecoming shine brighter.

BOLINGBROKE. No, every dull step I take will only remind me how much of the world lies between me and the jewels I love. Will I not have to serve a long apprenticeship in foreign travel? And in the end, once I have earned my freedom, will I have nothing to boast of except that I was a journeyman in the trade of grief?

GAUNT. To a wise man, every place the sun shines on is a port and a happy harbor. Let your need teach you to think like this: there is no virtue like making the best of necessity. Do not think the King banished you. Think that you banished the King. Misery weighs heavier on the man it sees bearing it weakly. Go, and tell yourself that I sent you out to win honor, and that the King did not exile you. Or imagine that a deadly plague hangs in our air, and you are escaping to a healthier climate. Whatever your soul holds dear, imagine it lies in the direction you are going, not where you came from. Imagine the singing birds are musicians, and the grass you walk on is the floor of the royal court strewn with rushes. Imagine the flowers are beautiful ladies, and your steps are nothing more than a pleasant measure or a dance. Snarling sorrow has less power to bite a man who laughs at it and treats it lightly.

BOLINGBROKE. Oh, who can hold fire in his hand by thinking about the frozen Caucasus mountains? Who can satisfy the sharp edge of hunger just by imagining a feast? Who can roll naked in December snow by thinking about imaginary summer heat? Oh no, thinking of the good only makes us feel the bad more sharply. Cruel sorrow’s tooth never hurts more than when it bites into the wound but does not lance it and let it drain.
GAUNT. Come, come, my son, I will see you on your way. If I had your youth and your reason, I would not stay here.

BOLINGBROKE. Then farewell, English ground. Goodbye, sweet soil, my mother and my nurse, who still carries me! Wherever I wander, I can boast of this: though I am banished, I am still a true-born Englishman.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 4 — London. A Room in the King’s Castle
paragraphs: [King Richard, Green and Bagot enter through one door, and Aumerle through another.]
KING RICHARD. Yes, we noticed that.—Cousin Aumerle, how far did you escort high-and-mighty Hereford on his way?
AUMERLE. I took high Hereford, if that is what you call him, only as far as the nearest highway, and I left him there.
KING RICHARD. And tell me, how many tears were shed at the parting?
AUMERLE. Honestly, I shed none, except that the northeast wind was blowing bitterly in our faces. It made my eyes water, and so by accident a tear decorated our empty goodbye.
KING RICHARD. What did our cousin say when you parted from him?

AUMERLE. He said “Farewell.” My heart refused to let my tongue cheapen that word by saying it back. So it taught me a trick: I pretended to be so overcome with grief that my words seemed buried in the grave of my sorrow. Believe me, if the word “farewell” could have made the hours longer and added years to his short exile, I would have given him a whole book of farewells. But since it could not, he got none from me.

KING RICHARD. He is our cousin, cousin. But it is doubtful, when time calls him home from exile, whether our relative will come home to see his friends. Bushy, Bagot here, Green and I all watched how he courted the common people. He seemed to dive into their hearts with humble, friendly courtesy. He wasted so much respect on low servants, and won over poor workmen with clever smiles and by bearing his bad luck so patiently. It was as if he meant to take their love with him into exile. Off came his cap to a woman selling oysters. A couple of cart drivers wished him God’s speed, and he paid them the tribute of a bended knee. He said, “Thank you, my countrymen, my loving friends,” as if our England belonged to him by right of succession, and he were our subjects’ next hope for king.

GREEN. Well, he is gone, and these worries can go with him. Now, my lord, about the rebels who are holding out in Ireland. We must take quick action before more delay gives them more ways to gain at your highness’s expense.

KING RICHARD. We will go to this war in person ourselves. Our treasury has grown rather light because our court is too large and we have been too generous with gifts. So we are forced to lease out our royal kingdom, and the rent from it will pay for the business at hand. If that is not enough, our deputies at home will have blank tax orders. When they find out which men are rich, they will write in large sums of gold beside those names. Then they will send the money after us to cover our needs. We are leaving for Ireland at once.
[Bushy enters.]
Bushy, what is the news?
BUSHY. Old John of Gaunt is seriously ill, my lord. It came on suddenly, and he has sent a messenger in a hurry to beg your Majesty to visit him.
KING RICHARD. Where is he?
BUSHY. At Ely House.

KING RICHARD. God, put the idea into his doctor’s head to help him into his grave right away! The lining of his money chests will make coats to dress our soldiers for these Irish wars. Come, gentlemen, let’s all go visit him. Pray to God that we hurry and still get there too late!
ALL. Amen!
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — London. An Apartment in Ely House
paragraphs: [Gaunt lies on a couch. The Duke of York and others stand beside him.]
GAUNT. Will the King come, so that I can spend my last breath giving sound advice to his reckless youth?
YORK. Do not upset yourself or strain your breath. Advice reaches his ear for nothing.

GAUNT. Oh, but they say the words of dying men command attention like deep music. When a man has few words left, he seldom wastes them. Those who speak in pain speak the truth. A man who will never speak again is listened to more than those whom youth and comfort have taught to flatter. People pay more attention to how men die than to how they lived. A setting sun, the last notes of music and the last taste of something sweet are the sweetest of all. They stay in the memory longer than things long past. Richard would not listen to my advice while I lived, but the sad words of my death may still unblock his deaf ears.

YORK. No, his ears are stuffed with other flattering sounds. There is praise, which even the wise are fond of. There are dirty verses, whose poisonous sound the open ears of youth always listen to. And there are reports of the latest fashions in proud Italy, whose manners our backward, copycat nation keeps limping after in cheap imitation. Whenever the world produces some new silliness—and as long as it is new, nobody cares how vile it is—is there any that is not quickly buzzed into his ears? So advice comes far too late to be heard when desire rebels against reason. Do not try to steer a man who insists on choosing his own path. You are short of breath, and you will lose what breath you have.

GAUNT. I feel like a prophet who has just been inspired, and as I die I predict this about him. His wild, fierce blaze of reckless living cannot last, because violent fires soon burn themselves out. Light showers last a long time, but sudden storms are short. A man who spurs his horse too hard too early tires early. Food chokes the man who eats it too greedily. Shallow vanity is a greedy cormorant that is never full, and once it has used up everything it has, it soon feeds on itself. This royal throne of kings, this island ruled by a scepter, this land of majesty, this home of the war god Mars! This second Eden, this half-paradise, this fortress Nature built for herself against disease and the hand of war! This happy race of men, this little world, this precious stone set in the silver sea! The sea serves it as a wall, or as a moat defending a house, against the envy of less fortunate lands. This blessed plot, this earth, this realm, this England! This nurse, this fertile womb of royal kings, who were feared for their ancestry and famous for their birth! Their deeds are famous far from home, for Christian service and true knighthood. They are as famous as the tomb of the world’s ransom, blessed Mary’s Son, in stubborn Judea. This land of such dear souls, this dear, dear land, dear for its reputation around the world, is now leased out like an apartment or a worthless farm. It kills me to say it. England, ringed by the triumphant sea, whose rocky shore beats back the jealous attacks of the watery sea god Neptune, is now ringed with shame. It is bound in with inky blots and rotten paper contracts. That England, which used to conquer other countries, has made a shameful conquest of itself. Ah, if only this scandal would vanish when my life does, how happy my coming death would be!
[King Richard and the Queen enter, with Aumerle, Bushy, Green, Bagot, Ross and Willoughby.]
YORK. The King has come. Go easy on his youth, because young hot-blooded colts only get wilder when you provoke them.
QUEEN. How is our noble uncle, Lancaster?
KING RICHARD. How are you, man? How are things with old Gaunt?

GAUNT. Oh, how well that name suits my condition! Old Gaunt indeed, and gaunt because I’m old. Grief has kept a long, dreary fast inside me, and who can go without food and not turn gaunt? I have stayed awake a long time watching over sleeping England. Staying awake makes you thin, and thinness is nothing but gauntness. The pleasure some fathers feast on is the one thing I’ve been made to fast from—I mean the sight of my children’s faces. By keeping me from that food, you have made me gaunt. I am gaunt and ready for the grave, as gaunt as a grave itself, whose hollow belly receives nothing but bones.
KING RICHARD. Can sick men really play such clever games with their own names?
GAUNT. No, it’s misery that amuses itself by mocking itself. Since you are trying to kill my name by killing my son’s future, I mock my own name, great king, to flatter you.
KING RICHARD. Should dying men flatter the living?
GAUNT. No, no, it’s living men who flatter the dying.
KING RICHARD. You are the one dying now, and you say you’re flattering me.
GAUNT. Oh, no, you are the one dying, even though I am the sicker man.
KING RICHARD. I am healthy, I’m breathing, and I can see that you are ill.

GAUNT. Well, God who made me knows that I see you badly. I am too ill myself to see well, and what I see in you is illness. Your deathbed is as large as your whole country, where you lie sick in reputation. And you, a far too careless patient, hand over your sacred, anointed body to the care of the same doctors who wounded you in the first place. A thousand flatterers sit inside your crown, which is no bigger around than your head. And yet, though they are caged in such a small circle, the waste they cause is just as large as your whole land. Oh, if your grandfather had seen with a prophet’s eye how his son’s son would destroy his sons, he would have put your shame out of your reach. He would have deposed you before you ever came into possession of the throne. Now that you possess it, you are deposing yourself. Why, cousin, even if you ruled the whole world, it would be shameful to lease out this land. But since this land is the only world you have, isn’t it more than shameful to disgrace it like this? You are England’s landlord now, not its king. Your royal status under the law is now a slave to the law, and you—

KING RICHARD. You crazy, half-witted fool! You take advantage of a sick man’s privileges and dare to use your cold lecture to make my cheek go pale with anger. You chase the royal blood out of its natural home in my face. Now, by the true majesty of my throne, if you weren’t the brother of great Edward’s son, this tongue that rattles on so freely in your head would send your head rolling off your disrespectful shoulders.

GAUNT. Oh, don’t spare me, my brother Edward’s son, just because I was the son of his father, Edward. Like the young pelican that feeds on its mother’s blood, you have already drained that blood and drunkenly guzzled it down. My brother Gloucester, a plain, well-meaning soul—may good things come to him among the blessed souls in heaven!—is proof enough and a good witness that you don’t care about spilling Edward’s blood. Let your unkindness join forces with the sickness I already have. Like bent old age, let it cut down at once a flower that has been withering far too long. Live on in your shame, but may that shame not die with you! May these words torment you from now on! Take me to my bed, and then to my grave. Let those who have love and honor want to live.
[He exits, carried off by his attendants.]
KING RICHARD. And let those who have old age and sulkiness die. You have both, and both belong in the grave.

YORK. I beg your Majesty to blame his words on the stubborn sickness and old age in him. I swear on my life that he loves you and holds you as dear as he would Harry, Duke of Hereford, if he were here.
KING RICHARD. Right, you’re correct. His love for me is like Hereford’s, and mine for them is like theirs for me. So let everything be just as it is.
[Northumberland enters.]
NORTHUMBERLAND. My lord, old Gaunt sends his respects to your Majesty.
KING RICHARD. What does he say?
NORTHUMBERLAND. No, nothing. Everything has been said. His tongue is now an instrument with no strings. Old Lancaster has used up his words, his life, and everything.
YORK. May York be the next to go bankrupt like that! Death may be poor, but it puts an end to human suffering.

KING RICHARD. The ripest fruit falls first, and so has he. His time is over, but our journey through life must go on. So much for that. Now for our wars in Ireland. We must root out those rough, shaggy-haired Irish foot soldiers. They live like poison in a land where no other poison is allowed to live. And since these great affairs require some expense, we are seizing for our own use all the silverware, money, income, and movable goods that our uncle Gaunt owned.

YORK. How long must I be patient? Ah, how long will my gentle sense of duty make me put up with wrongs? Gloucester’s death and Hereford’s banishment never made me scowl. Neither did Gaunt’s scolding, the wrongs done to ordinary English people, or your blocking poor Bolingbroke’s marriage, or my own disgrace. None of it ever made me sour my patient face or frown once at my king. I am the last of noble Edward’s sons, and your father, the Prince of Wales, was the first of them. No lion ever raged more fiercely in war, and no gentle lamb was ever milder in peace, than that young and princely gentleman. You have his face, for he looked just like you when he was your age. But when he frowned, it was against the French, not against his friends. His noble hand won what he spent, and he did not spend what his triumphant father’s hand had won. His hands were not guilty of his relatives’ blood. They were bloody only with the blood of his family’s enemies. Oh, Richard! York is too overcome with grief, or else he would never make this comparison.
KING RICHARD. Why, uncle, what’s wrong?

YORK. Oh, my lord, forgive me if you like. If not, I’m happy not to be forgiven, and I’ll accept that too. Are you trying to seize and grab into your own hands the royal privileges and rights of the banished Hereford? Isn’t Gaunt dead? And isn’t Hereford alive? Wasn’t Gaunt a just man? And isn’t Harry loyal? Didn’t the one deserve to have an heir? Isn’t his heir a deserving son? If you take Hereford’s rights away, you might as well take away Time’s own charters and customary rights. Then don’t let tomorrow follow today. Then don’t be yourself, because how are you king except by proper descent and succession? Now, before God—and God forbid that I’m right!—suppose you wrongfully seize Hereford’s rights. Suppose you cancel the royal documents that let his lawyers claim his inheritance, and you refuse his offer of homage. Then you will bring a thousand dangers down on your head. You will lose a thousand hearts that wish you well. And you will goad my gentle patience into thoughts that honor and loyalty must never think.
KING RICHARD. Think whatever you like. We are seizing his silverware, his goods, his money, and his lands.
YORK. I won’t be here to watch it. My lord, goodbye. No one can tell what will come of this. But we can see from bad conduct that the results can never turn out well.
[He exits.]

KING RICHARD. Bushy, go straight to the Earl of Wiltshire. Tell him to come to me at Ely House to take care of this business. Tomorrow we leave for Ireland, and it’s high time, I believe. In our absence we appoint our uncle York Lord Governor of England, because he is fair and has always loved us well. Come on, my queen. Tomorrow we must part. Be cheerful, because our time together is short.
[The King, Queen, Bushy, Aumerle, Green, and Bagot exit.]
NORTHUMBERLAND. Well, lords, the Duke of Lancaster is dead.
ROSS. And alive too, since his son is now Duke.
WILLOUGHBY. Only in title, though, not in income.
NORTHUMBERLAND. He would be rich in both if there were any justice.
ROSS. My heart is full, but it will have to break in silence before I unload it by speaking freely.
NORTHUMBERLAND. No, say what you think. And if anyone repeats your words to harm you, may he never speak again!
WILLOUGHBY. Does what you want to say concern the Duke of Hereford? If so, out with it boldly, man. My ears are quick to hear anything good for him.
ROSS. There’s nothing good I can do for him, unless you call it good to pity him. He has been robbed and stripped of his inheritance, as if castrated.

NORTHUMBERLAND. Now, before God, it’s a shame that such wrongs are inflicted on him, a royal prince, and on many more men of noble blood in this decaying country. The King is not himself. He is shamefully led around by flatterers. Whatever accusations they make out of pure hatred against any of us, the King will harshly pursue against us, our lives, our children, and our heirs.
ROSS. He has stripped the common people with heavy taxes and completely lost their hearts. He has fined the nobles over old quarrels and completely lost their hearts too.

WILLOUGHBY. And new ways of squeezing out money are invented every day, like blank checks, forced gifts called benevolences, and who knows what else. But in God’s name, what is happening to all this money?

NORTHUMBERLAND. War hasn’t used it up, because he hasn’t fought any wars. Instead he has shamefully given away by compromise what his ancestors won with blows. He has spent more in peacetime than they spent in war.
ROSS. The Earl of Wiltshire has leased the kingdom to run for profit.
WILLOUGHBY. The King has gone bankrupt like a ruined man.
NORTHUMBERLAND. Disgrace and ruin are hanging over him.
ROSS. In spite of his heavy taxes, he has no money for these Irish wars except what he gets by robbing the banished Duke.

NORTHUMBERLAND. And the Duke is his own noble relative. What a degenerate king! But, lords, we hear this terrible storm howling, and still we look for no shelter to escape it. We see the wind pressing hard on our sails, and yet we don’t lower them. We just die thinking we’re safe.
ROSS. We can see the very shipwreck we are going to suffer. And the danger can no longer be avoided, because we have put up with the things that are causing our wreck.
NORTHUMBERLAND. That’s not so. Even through the hollow eye sockets of death I can see life peeping out. But I don’t dare say how close the news that will comfort us is.
WILLOUGHBY. No, share your thoughts with us, as we have shared ours with you.
ROSS. Speak confidently, Northumberland. The three of us are just like one person, you yourself. So when you speak to us, your words are as private as your thoughts. So be bold.

NORTHUMBERLAND. Then here it is. I have received news from Le Port Blanc, a bay in Brittany. Harry, Duke of Hereford, is coming, along with Rainold Lord Cobham, who recently escaped from the Duke of Exeter. So is his brother, who was until recently Archbishop of Canterbury. So are Sir Thomas Erpingham, Sir John Ramston, Sir John Norbery, Sir Robert Waterton, and Francis Coint. The Duke of Brittany has equipped all of them well with eight large ships and three thousand soldiers. They are heading here as fast as they can and plan to land on our northern shore soon. Maybe they would have landed already, but they are waiting for the King to leave for Ireland first. So if we want to throw off the yoke that makes us slaves, we must act. We must mend the broken wing of our drooping country with new feathers. We must buy the stained crown back from the pawnbroker. We must wipe off the dust that hides the gold on our scepter, and make high majesty look like itself again. If so, ride with me at full speed to Ravenspurgh. But if you lose your nerve and are afraid to do it, stay here and keep quiet, and I will go alone.
ROSS. To horse, to horse! Save your doubts for those who are afraid.
WILLOUGHBY. As long as my horse holds out, I will be there first.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — The Same. A Room in the Castle
paragraphs: [The Queen, Bushy, and Bagot enter.]
BUSHY. Madam, your Majesty is far too sad. When you said goodbye to the King, you promised to put aside this heavy sadness that harms your health and to adopt a cheerful mood.

QUEEN. I did that to please the King. To please myself, I can’t do it. Yet I know of no reason why I should welcome a guest like grief, except for saying goodbye to a guest as sweet as my sweet Richard. And yet again it seems to me that some sorrow not yet born, ripe in the womb of Fortune, is coming toward me. My inner soul trembles at nothing. It grieves over something more than over parting from my lord the King.

BUSHY. Every real grief has twenty shadows that look like grief itself but are not. The eye of sorrow, glazed over with blinding tears, splits one whole thing into many objects. It is like those trick pictures that show nothing but a jumble when you look at them straight on, but show a clear shape when you look at them from an angle. In the same way, your sweet Majesty, looking at your husband’s departure from a skewed angle, finds shapes of grief beyond the departure itself to weep over. Seen as it really is, it is nothing but shadows of what it isn’t. So, most gracious Queen, weep for nothing more than your husband’s departure. There is nothing more to see. Or if there is, it is seen with the false eye of sorrow, which weeps over imaginary things as if they were real.

QUEEN. That may be so, but my inner soul tells me it is otherwise. Whatever it is, I can’t help being sad. I am so heavily sad that, though I try to think of nothing, the very thought of nothing makes me faint and shrink under its heavy weight.
BUSHY. It’s nothing but your imagination, my gracious lady.

QUEEN. It’s anything but that. Imagined grief always comes from some earlier, real grief, like a child from its ancestor. Mine isn’t like that. Either nothing has given birth to my grief over something, or else there is something in the nothing that I grieve for. It’s like an inheritance I own but haven’t yet received. But what it is, I don’t yet know, and I can’t name it. It’s a nameless sorrow, I tell you.
[Green enters.]
GREEN. God save your Majesty! And good to see you, gentlemen. I hope the King hasn’t sailed for Ireland yet.
QUEEN. Why do you hope that? It would be better to hope that he has, because his plans require speed, and his speed gives us good hope. So why do you hope he hasn’t sailed?

GREEN. Because then he, our hope, could have brought his army back. He could have driven to despair the hopes of an enemy who has firmly set foot in this country. The banished Bolingbroke has called himself back from exile. He has arrived safely at Ravenspurgh with his weapons raised.
QUEEN. Now God in heaven forbid!

GREEN. Ah, madam, it’s all too true. And what’s worse, Lord Northumberland, his son young Harry Percy, and the Lords Ross, Beaumond, and Willoughby have all run off to join him, with all their powerful friends.
BUSHY. Why haven’t you declared Northumberland and all the rest of that rebel faction traitors?
GREEN. We have. And because of that, the Earl of Worcester has broken his staff of office and resigned as steward. All the household servants have fled with him to Bolingbroke.

QUEEN. So, Green, you are the midwife who has delivered my sorrow, and Bolingbroke is the gloomy child my sorrow has given birth to. Now my soul has given birth to its monster. And I, a mother gasping after the delivery, have piled sorrow on sorrow and grief on grief.
BUSHY. Don’t despair, madam.

QUEEN. Who will stop me? I will despair and be the enemy of cheating hope. Hope is a flatterer, a parasite, something that holds death back. Death would gently untie the bonds of life, but false hope drags those bonds out when things are at their worst.
[York enters.]
GREEN. Here comes the Duke of York.
QUEEN. He has the signs of war around his old neck. Oh, his face is full of worried business! Uncle, for God’s sake, say something comforting.

YORK. If I did, I would be lying about what I think. Comfort is in heaven, and we are on earth, where nothing lives but troubles, worries, and grief. Your husband has gone far away to save his territory over there, while others come to make him lose it here at home. I have been left here to prop up his country, and I am so weak with age that I can’t even hold myself up. Now comes the sickness that his excesses have caused. Now he will test the friends who flattered him.
[A Servant enters.]
SERVINGMAN. My lord, your son had already left before I got there.

YORK. He had? Well, then! Let everything go however it will! The nobles have fled, and the common people are indifferent. I’m afraid they will rebel and join Hereford’s side. You there, go to Plashy, to my sister-in-law, the Duchess of Gloucester. Tell her to send me a thousand pounds right away. Wait, take my ring.
SERVINGMAN. My lord, I forgot to tell your lordship. Today, as I passed by, I stopped in there— But it will upset you if I tell you the rest.
YORK. What is it, you rascal?
SERVINGMAN. The Duchess died an hour before I got there.

YORK. God have mercy, what a flood of troubles comes rushing over this miserable country all at once! I don’t know what to do. I wish to God the King had cut off my head along with my brother’s, as long as it wasn’t my disloyalty that drove him to it. What, have no messengers been sent to Ireland? How are we going to get money for these wars? Come, sister—I mean cousin, please forgive me. Go, man, go home. Get some carts and bring away the armor that’s there.
[The Servant exits.]

Gentlemen, will you go and gather troops? If I know how or in what way to manage these affairs that have been shoved into my hands in such disorder, never believe me again. Both of them are my relatives. One is my king, whom both my oath and my duty tell me to defend. The other is also my relative, whom the King has wronged, and my conscience and family ties tell me to set things right for him. Well, we have to do something. Come, cousin, I’ll find a place for you. Gentlemen, go and gather your men, and meet me right away at Berkeley Castle. I ought to go to Plashy too, but there isn’t time. Everything is out of balance, and everything is left in total chaos.
[York and the Queen exit.]
BUSHY. The wind is favorable for sending news to Ireland, but none comes back. It’s completely impossible for us to raise an army as large as the enemy’s.
GREEN. Besides, being close to the King in his affection puts us close to the hatred of those who don’t love the King.
BAGOT. And that means the fickle common people, because their love lies in their wallets. Whoever empties their wallets fills their hearts with deadly hatred by just as much.
BUSHY. And for that, the King is condemned by everyone.
BAGOT. If it’s up to them to pass judgment, then we are condemned too, because we have always been close to the King.
GREEN. Well, I’m going straight to Bristol Castle for safety. The Earl of Wiltshire is already there.
BUSHY. I’ll go there with you. The hateful common people won’t do much for us except tear us all to pieces like dogs. Will you come along with us?
BAGOT. No, I’ll go to Ireland, to his Majesty. Goodbye. If the heart’s forebodings aren’t empty, we three are parting here and will never meet again.
BUSHY. That depends on whether York succeeds in beating Bolingbroke back.

GREEN. Alas, poor Duke! The job he’s taking on is like counting grains of sand or drinking the oceans dry. For every man who fights on his side, thousands will run away. Goodbye, all at once—once, for all, and forever.
BUSHY. Well, we may meet again.
BAGOT. I’m afraid we never will.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — The Wolds in Gloucestershire
paragraphs: [Bolingbroke and Northumberland enter with their troops.]
BOLINGBROKE. My lord, how far is it to Berkeley now?

NORTHUMBERLAND. Believe me, noble lord, I’m a stranger here in Gloucestershire. These high, wild hills and rough, uneven roads stretch out our miles and make them exhausting. And yet your pleasant conversation has been like sugar, making the hard road sweet and delightful. But I keep thinking what a weary road Ross and Willoughby will find it from Ravenspurgh to Cotswold without your company. I swear your company has made the boredom and the length of my journey pass very pleasantly. But their journey is sweetened by the hope of having what I already have. And hoping for joy is hardly less joyful than having that hope fulfilled. Because of that hope, those tired lords will make their road seem as short as mine has seemed, thanks to what I have: your noble company.
BOLINGBROKE. My company is worth much less than your kind words. But who’s coming here?
[Harry Percy enters.]
NORTHUMBERLAND. It’s my son, young Harry Percy, sent from my brother Worcester—from wherever he is now. Harry, how is your uncle?
PERCY. My lord, I thought I would learn how he was from you.
NORTHUMBERLAND. Why, isn’t he with the Queen?
PERCY. No, my good lord. He has left the court, broken his staff of office, and dismissed the King’s household staff.
NORTHUMBERLAND. What was his reason? He hadn’t decided anything like that the last time we spoke.

PERCY. It was because your lordship was proclaimed a traitor. But he, my lord, has gone to Ravenspurgh to offer his service to the Duke of Hereford. He sent me by way of Berkeley to find out what forces the Duke of York had raised there. Then I was told to go on to Ravenspurgh.
NORTHUMBERLAND. Have you forgotten the Duke of Hereford, boy?
PERCY. No, my good lord, because you can’t forget something you never remembered. As far as I know, I’ve never laid eyes on him in my life.
NORTHUMBERLAND. Then get to know him now. This is the Duke.
PERCY. My gracious lord, I offer you my service. It’s young, raw, and untested for now. But as I grow older, it will ripen and strengthen into service that is more proven and deserving.

BOLINGBROKE. Thank you, gentle Percy. And be sure of this: nothing makes me happier than having a soul that remembers my good friends. As my fortune ripens along with your love, it will always reward your true love. My heart makes this promise, and with my hand I seal it.
NORTHUMBERLAND. How far is it to Berkeley? And what’s keeping good old York busy there with his soldiers?

PERCY. There’s the castle, by that clump of trees over there. I’ve heard it’s manned by three hundred men. Inside are the Lords of York, Berkeley, and Seymour. There’s no one else of any name or noble rank.
[Ross and Willoughby enter.]
NORTHUMBERLAND. Here come the Lords of Ross and Willoughby, bloody from spurring their horses and red-faced from riding so fast.

BOLINGBROKE. Welcome, my lords. I know your loyalty is following a banished traitor. All my wealth right now is nothing but thanks you can’t touch. When it grows richer, it will be the reward for your love and your labor.
ROSS. Being with you makes us rich, most noble lord.
WILLOUGHBY. And it far outweighs the effort it took us to get here.
BOLINGBROKE. Thanks, always thanks—the only treasury the poor have. Until my infant fortune grows up, thanks will have to stand in for my generosity. But who’s coming here?
[Berkeley enters.]
NORTHUMBERLAND. It’s my Lord of Berkeley, I think.
BERKELEY. My Lord of Hereford, I have a message for you.
BOLINGBROKE. My lord, I answer only to “Lancaster.” I’ve come to England to claim that name. I must hear that title from your lips before I reply to anything you say.

BERKELEY. Don’t misunderstand me, my lord. I don’t mean to erase a single one of your titles. I come to you, my lord—whatever lord you want to be called—from the most gracious regent of this country, the Duke of York. He wants to know what drives you to take advantage of the King’s absence and to frighten our peaceful land with weapons you took up on your own.
[York enters with attendants.]
BOLINGBROKE. I won’t need you to carry my words. Here comes his Grace himself. My noble uncle!
[He kneels.]
YORK. Show me a humble heart, not a bent knee. Kneeling like that is deceptive and false.
BOLINGBROKE. My gracious uncle—

YORK. Nonsense! Don’t call me your grace, and don’t call me uncle. I’m no traitor’s uncle, and the word “grace” in a graceless mouth is nothing but blasphemy. Why have those banished, forbidden legs of yours dared to touch even a speck of English soil? And more than that—why have they dared to march so many miles across her peaceful breast? Why do you frighten her pale-faced villages with war and with a display of hated weapons? Have you come because the anointed King is away? Why, you foolish boy, the King has left his power behind, and it lies here in my loyal heart. If only I were as young and hot-blooded as I was when brave Gaunt, your father, and I rescued the Black Prince, that young god of war, from the ranks of many thousands of Frenchmen! Oh, then how quickly this arm of mine, now a prisoner of palsy, would punish you and correct your offense!
BOLINGBROKE. My gracious uncle, tell me what my offense is. What is its nature, and where does it lie?
YORK. Its nature is the worst there is: outright rebellion and hateful treason. You are a banished man, and you’ve come back before your sentence has run out. You’ve come in arms, defying your king.

BOLINGBROKE. When I was banished, I was banished as Hereford. But now that I’ve come back, I come as Lancaster. And, noble uncle, I beg your Grace to look at the wrongs done to me with an unbiased eye. You are like a father to me, because I think I see old Gaunt alive in you. Then, my father, will you let me stand condemned as a wandering vagrant? Will you let my rights and royal privileges be torn from my arms by force and handed to spendthrift upstarts? Why was I born? If my cousin is King in England, then it must be granted that I am Duke of Lancaster. You have a son, Aumerle, my noble cousin. If you had died first and he’d been trampled like this, he would have found a father in his uncle Gaunt. Gaunt would have hunted down his wrongs and cornered them. I’m forbidden to claim my inheritance here, even though my legal documents give me the right to. My father’s goods have all been seized and sold, and the money has all been misused. What do you want me to do? I’m a subject, and I demand the law. I’m not allowed lawyers to plead for me. So I’m making my claim in person to my inheritance, which comes to me by rightful descent.
NORTHUMBERLAND. The noble Duke has been treated very badly.
ROSS. It’s your Grace’s duty to see that he gets justice.
WILLOUGHBY. Low-born men have been made great with his property.

YORK. Lords of England, let me tell you this. I have felt for my cousin’s wrongs, and I’ve worked as hard as I could to get him justice. But to come like this, in arms and defiant, to carve out his own share and cut his own path, seeking right by doing wrong—that cannot be allowed. And all of you who help him this way are encouraging rebellion, and you’re all rebels.
NORTHUMBERLAND. The noble Duke has sworn that he has come only for what is his own. We have all sworn firmly to help him get his rights. May whoever breaks that oath never see joy!

YORK. Well, well, I can see where these arms will lead. I have to admit I can’t do anything about it, because my forces are weak and badly equipped. But if I could, I swear by God who gave me life, I would arrest you all and make you bow to the King’s royal mercy. But since I can’t, let it be known that I stay neutral. So goodbye—unless you’d like to come into the castle and rest there tonight.

BOLINGBROKE. That’s an offer we will accept, uncle. But we must persuade your Grace to go with us to Bristol Castle. They say it’s held by Bushy, Bagot, and their accomplices. They are the caterpillars eating up the country, and I’ve sworn to weed them out and pull them up.

YORK. Maybe I’ll go with you. But I’ll think it over, because I hate to break our country’s laws. You are welcome here neither as friends nor as enemies. Things that can’t be fixed are no longer my concern.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 4 — A camp in Wales
paragraphs: [The Earl of Salisbury and a Welsh Captain enter.]
CAPTAIN. My Lord of Salisbury, we’ve waited ten days and have barely kept our countrymen together. And still we hear no news from the King. So we’re going to disband. Goodbye.
SALISBURY. Stay one more day, my trusty Welshman. The King is putting all his trust in you.

CAPTAIN. People think the King is dead. We won’t stay. The bay trees in our country have all withered, and meteors are frightening the fixed stars in the sky. The pale-faced moon looks blood-red on the earth, and gaunt prophets whisper of terrible change. Rich men look gloomy, while thugs dance and leap. The rich are afraid to lose what they have, and the thugs hope to enjoy it through violence and war. These signs come before the death or fall of kings. Goodbye. Our countrymen have run off and fled, convinced that Richard, their king, is dead.
[He exits.]

SALISBURY. Ah, Richard! With the eyes of a heavy heart I see your glory falling like a shooting star from the sky to the lowly earth. Your sun sets weeping in the humble west, foretelling storms, sorrow, and unrest to come. Your friends have fled to serve your enemies, and all fortune runs against your good.
[He exits.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — Bristol. Bolingbroke’s camp
paragraphs: [Bolingbroke, York, Northumberland, Harry Percy, Willoughby, and Ross enter. Officers follow behind with Bushy and Green as prisoners.]

BOLINGBROKE. Bring these men forward. Bushy and Green, your souls must leave your bodies very soon, so I won’t torment them by dwelling on your wicked lives. That would be uncharitable. Still, to wash your blood off my hands, I will lay out here, in front of everyone, some of the reasons you must die. You have misled a prince, a royal king, a fortunate gentleman in birth and looks. You have made him unfortunate and disfigured him completely. With your sinful company you have, in effect, divorced him from his queen. You broke up their royal marriage bed. You stained the beauty of a lovely queen’s cheeks with tears that your foul wrongs drew from her eyes. I myself am a prince by birth, close to the King in blood. I was close to him in love too, until you made him misjudge me. I have bowed my neck under your injuries and sighed my English breath into foreign clouds, eating the bitter bread of banishment. Meanwhile you have fed on my estates. You opened up my private parks and cut down the trees in my forests. You tore my family coat of arms from my own windows and scratched out my emblems. You left me no sign to show the world I am a gentleman except what people think of me and the blood in my veins. This and much more—much more than twice all this—condemns you to death. See them handed over to execution and the hand of death.
BUSHY. The blow of death is more welcome to me than Bolingbroke is to England. Lords, goodbye.
GREEN. My comfort is that heaven will take our souls and punish injustice with the torments of hell.
BOLINGBROKE. My Lord Northumberland, see that they are executed.
[Northumberland and others exit with Bushy and Green.]
Uncle, you say the Queen is staying at your house. For God’s sake, see that she is treated well. Tell her I send her my warm regards. Make especially sure my greetings reach her.
YORK. I’ve sent one of my gentlemen to her with letters fully describing your goodwill toward her.
BOLINGBROKE. Thank you, gentle uncle. Come, lords, let’s go fight Glendower and his accomplices. A little while for work, and then a holiday.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — The coast of Wales. A castle in view
paragraphs: [A flourish of drums and trumpets. King Richard, the Bishop of Carlisle, Aumerle, and soldiers enter.]
KING RICHARD. Is this the castle nearby they call Barkloughly?
AUMERLE. Yes, my lord. How does your Grace like the air after being tossed around on the rough seas?

KING RICHARD. I have to like it. I weep for joy to stand on my kingdom again. Dear earth, I greet you with my hand, though rebels wound you with their horses’ hooves. A mother long separated from her child plays tenderly with her tears and smiles when they meet. In the same way, weeping and smiling, I greet you, my earth, and caress you with my royal hands. Don’t feed your sovereign’s enemy, my gentle earth, and don’t comfort his greedy appetite with your sweet things. Instead, let your spiders, who suck up your poison, and your slow, heavy toads lie in their path. Let them trouble the treacherous feet that trample you with usurping steps. Grow stinging nettles for my enemies. And when they pick a flower from your breast, guard it, I beg you, with a hidden snake. Let its forked tongue, with one deadly touch, kill your sovereign’s enemies. Don’t laugh at me for pleading with things that can’t feel, my lords. This earth will come to have feelings, and these stones will turn into armed soldiers, before her native king falls to foul rebellion’s weapons.

CARLISLE. Don’t be afraid, my lord. The Power that made you king has the power to keep you king in spite of everything. But we must take hold of the means heaven gives us and not neglect them. Otherwise heaven wants one thing and we refuse it. Then we’re turning down heaven’s offer—the help and remedy it holds out to us.
AUMERLE. He means, my lord, that we are too slack. Meanwhile, because we feel so safe, Bolingbroke grows strong and great in wealth and power.

KING RICHARD. Discouraging cousin, don’t you know this? When the searching eye of heaven, the sun, is hidden behind the earth and lighting the world below, then thieves and robbers roam around here unseen, boldly committing murders and outrages. But when the sun comes up from under this earthly ball, it sets the proud tops of the eastern pines on fire. It shoots its light into every guilty hole. Then murders, treasons, and hateful sins have the cloak of night pulled off their backs. They stand bare and naked, trembling at themselves. In the same way, this thief, this traitor, Bolingbroke, has been partying in the dark all this time while we were wandering on the other side of the world. When he sees us rising on our throne like the sun in the east, his treasons will blush in his face. He won’t be able to stand the sight of day, but will be frightened of himself and tremble at his sin. Not all the water in the rough, wild sea can wash the holy oil off an anointed king. The breath of mortal men can’t remove from power the deputy chosen by the Lord. For every man Bolingbroke has forced to raise sharp steel against our golden crown, God has a glorious angel in heavenly pay to fight for his Richard. So if angels fight, weak men must fall, because heaven always protects the right.
[Salisbury enters.]
Welcome, my lord. How far away is your army?

SALISBURY. No nearer or farther away, my gracious lord, than this weak arm. Despair guides my tongue and tells me to speak of nothing but hopelessness. I’m afraid, noble lord, that being one day too late has darkened all your happy days on earth. Oh, call back yesterday, make time turn back, and you would have twelve thousand fighting men! Today, today, this unlucky day, too late, overthrows your joys, friends, fortune, and position. All the Welshmen heard you were dead, and they have gone over to Bolingbroke, scattered, and fled.
AUMERLE. Take heart, my liege. Why does your Grace look so pale?

KING RICHARD. Just a moment ago the blood of twenty thousand men glowed proudly in my face, and now they’ve fled. Until that much blood comes back to it, don’t I have reason to look pale and dead? Everyone who wants to be safe, run from my side, because time has stained my pride.
AUMERLE. Take heart, my liege. Remember who you are.

KING RICHARD. I had forgotten myself. Am I not king? Wake up, you cowardly majesty! You’re asleep! Isn’t the King’s name worth twenty thousand names? Arm yourself, arm yourself, my name! A puny subject is attacking your great glory. Don’t look at the ground, you favorites of a king. Aren’t we high? Then let our thoughts be high. I know my uncle York has enough forces to serve our purpose. But who’s coming here?
[Sir Stephen Scroop enters.]
SCROOP. May more health and happiness come to my liege than my sorrow-tuned tongue can bring him.

KING RICHARD. My ear is open and my heart is ready. The worst you can tell me is a worldly loss. Tell me, is my kingdom lost? Why, it was my burden, and what loss is it to be rid of a burden? Is Bolingbroke trying to be as great as we are? He won’t be greater. If he serves God, we’ll serve Him too, and so be his equal. Are our subjects rebelling? We can’t fix that. They break faith with God as well as with us. Cry out sorrow, destruction, ruin, loss, decay. The worst is death, and death will have its day.

SCROOP. I’m glad your Highness is so well prepared to hear news of disaster. Bolingbroke’s fury has risen far beyond its bounds, like an unseasonable stormy day that makes the silver rivers flood their banks, as if the whole world had dissolved into tears. He is covering your frightened land with hard, bright steel and with hearts harder than steel. White-bearded old men have put helmets on their thin, bald heads to fight against your Majesty. Boys with high, girlish voices try to talk tough, and they strap their soft, womanish limbs into stiff, clumsy armor to fight against your crown. Even the old pensioners who are paid to pray for you are learning to bend their bows of yew—wood that kills twice, as poison and as weapon—against your rule. Yes, even women who spin thread are wielding rusty pikes against your throne. Both young and old are rebelling, and everything is going worse than I have the power to describe.

KING RICHARD. You tell such a terrible story too well, too well. Where is the Earl of Wiltshire? Where is Bagot? What has become of Bushy? Where is Green? How could they let the dangerous enemy pace out our territory with such untroubled steps? If we win, their heads will pay for it. I bet they have made peace with Bolingbroke.
SCROOP. They have certainly made peace with him, my lord.

KING RICHARD. Oh, villains! Vipers, damned beyond any salvation! Dogs, ready to fawn on any man who pats them! Snakes I warmed with my own heart’s blood, who now sting my heart! Three Judases, each one three times worse than Judas! They would make peace? Let terrible hell make war on their stained souls for this!

SCROOP. I see that sweet love, when it changes its nature, turns into the bitterest and deadliest hate. Take back your curses on their souls. They made their peace by losing their heads, not by shaking hands. The men you’re cursing have suffered death’s worst, most destructive wound. They lie low now, buried in the hollow ground.
AUMERLE. Are Bushy, Green and the Earl of Wiltshire dead?
SCROOP. Yes, all of them lost their heads at Bristol.
AUMERLE. Where is the Duke, my father, with his army?

KING RICHARD. It doesn’t matter where. Let no one speak of comfort! Let’s talk about graves, worms and epitaphs. Let’s make the dust our paper and, with our rainy eyes, write sorrow on the breast of the earth. Let’s choose executors and talk about wills. And yet, no—what can we leave to anyone except our deposed bodies, which go to the ground? Our lands, our lives, everything belongs to Bolingbroke. Nothing can we call our own except death, and that small patch of barren earth that covers our bones like a pie crust. For God’s sake, let’s sit on the ground and tell sad stories about the deaths of kings. Some were deposed, some killed in war, some haunted by the ghosts of those they deposed. Some were poisoned by their wives, some killed in their sleep—all of them murdered. Inside the hollow crown that circles a king’s mortal head, Death holds his court. That clown sits there, mocking the king’s majesty and grinning at his pomp. He allows the king a breath, a short scene on stage, to play the monarch, be feared and kill with a look. He fills him with self-importance and empty fantasies, as if this flesh that walls in our life were unbreakable brass. And when he has humored him like this, Death comes at last and bores through his castle wall with a little pin—and farewell, king! Put your hats back on. Don’t mock flesh and blood with solemn bowing. Throw away respect, tradition, formality and ceremonial duty, because you have misunderstood me all this time. I live on bread like you, feel need, taste grief and need friends. If I’m subject to all that, how can you tell me I am a king?

CARLISLE. My lord, wise men never sit and lament their troubles. They act at once to stop the causes of lament. Fear weakens your strength, so fearing the enemy only gives him strength out of your weakness. That way your own foolishness fights against you. If you’re afraid, you’ll be killed—fighting can bring nothing worse than that. To fight and die is to destroy death by dying bravely. To be afraid of dying is to pay death the tribute of a slave.
AUMERLE. My father has an army. Ask about him, and learn to make a whole body out of one limb.

KING RICHARD. You scold me rightly. Proud Bolingbroke, I’m coming to trade blows with you and settle which of us is doomed. This feverish fit of fear has passed. It’s an easy task to win back what is ours. Tell me, Scroop, where is our uncle with his army? Speak sweetly, man, even though your face looks sour.

SCROOP. People judge what the day’s weather will be by the color of the sky. In the same way, you can judge my news by my dull, heavy eyes. My tongue has an even heavier story to tell. I’m acting like a torturer, dragging out bit by bit the worst news that has to be spoken. Your uncle York has joined Bolingbroke. All your northern castles have surrendered, and all your southern noblemen have taken up arms on his side.

KING RICHARD. You’ve said enough. [To Aumerle.] Curse you, cousin, for leading me away from the sweet road I was taking to despair. What do you say now? What comfort do we have now? By heaven, I’ll hate forever anyone who tells me to take comfort again. Go to Flint Castle. I’ll waste away there. A king who is sorrow’s slave will obey sorrow like a king. Dismiss the army I have, and let them go plow land that still has some hope of growing something. I have none. Let no one say another word to change this, because advice is useless.
AUMERLE. My lord, just one word.
KING RICHARD. Anyone who wounds me with flattering words does me a double wrong. Dismiss my followers. Let them leave, going from Richard’s night to Bolingbroke’s bright day.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — Wales. Before Flint Castle
paragraphs: [Bolingbroke and his forces enter with drums and flags, along with Northumberland and others.]
BOLINGBROKE. So this report tells us that the Welsh troops have scattered, and Salisbury has gone to meet the King. The King recently landed on this coast with a few close friends.
NORTHUMBERLAND. That’s very good news, my lord. Richard is hiding his head not far from here.
YORK. It would be more fitting for Lord Northumberland to say “King Richard.” What a sad day it is when such a sacred king has to hide his head!
NORTHUMBERLAND. Your Grace misunderstands. I only left out his title to be brief.
YORK. There was a time when, if you had been so brief with him, he would have been just as brief with you. He would have shortened you by your whole head’s length for taking such liberties with his.
BOLINGBROKE. Uncle, don’t misjudge things more than you should.
YORK. And you, good cousin, don’t take more than you should, or you’ll make a mistake. Heaven is above our heads, watching.
BOLINGBROKE. I know that, uncle, and I don’t set myself against heaven’s will. But who is coming?
[Harry Percy enters.]
Welcome, Harry. What, won’t this castle surrender?
PERCY. My lord, the castle is royally defended against your entry.
BOLINGBROKE. Royally? Why, there’s no king inside, is there?
