PERCY. Yes, my good lord, there is a king inside. King Richard is within those walls of lime and stone. With him are Lord Aumerle, Lord Salisbury and Sir Stephen Scroop, as well as a highly respected clergyman. I can’t find out who he is.
NORTHUMBERLAND. Oh, it’s probably the Bishop of Carlisle.

BOLINGBROKE. [To Northumberland.] Noble lord, go to the rough walls of that old castle. Send a call for a parley through a brass trumpet into its crumbling ears, and deliver this message. Henry Bolingbroke kisses King Richard’s hand on both knees. He sends his loyalty and the true faith of his heart to the King’s royal person. He has come here to lay his weapons and his army at the King’s feet—on condition that his banishment is canceled and his lands are freely given back. If not, I’ll use the advantage of my strength. I’ll settle the summer dust with showers of blood rained from the wounds of slaughtered Englishmen. My humble, bowing duty will gently show how far it is from Bolingbroke’s mind that such a red storm should drench the fresh green lap of fair King Richard’s land. Go and tell him this, while we march here across the grassy carpet of this plain. Let’s march without the sound of threatening drums, so that from the castle’s crumbling battlements they can clearly see our fine equipment. I think King Richard and I should meet as terrifyingly as the elements of fire and water. When they collide with a thunderous shock, they tear the cloudy cheeks of the sky. Let him be the fire, and I’ll be the yielding water. Let the fury be his, while I rain my waters on the earth—on the earth, not on him. March on, and watch how King Richard looks.
[A trumpet sounds for a parley and is answered by a trumpet inside. Flourish. On the walls appear the King, the Bishop of Carlisle, Aumerle, Scroop and Salisbury.]

Look, look, King Richard appears himself. He is like the sun, red-faced and displeased, coming out of the fiery gateway of the east when it sees that jealous clouds are set on dimming its glory and staining the path of its bright journey to the west.
YORK. Still, he looks like a king. Look at his eye, as bright as an eagle’s. It flashes out commanding majesty. Alas, alas, what a sorrow that any harm should stain such a fine sight!

KING RICHARD. [To Northumberland.] We are astonished. We’ve stood here this long waiting for you to bend your knee in respect, because we thought we were your lawful king. And if we are, how dare your joints forget to pay the reverent duty owed to our presence? If we are not, show us the hand of God that has dismissed us from our office. We know well that no hand of flesh and bone can grip the sacred handle of our scepter without committing sacrilege, theft or usurpation. You may think that everyone has damaged their souls by turning away from us, as you have done. You may think we are poor and stripped of friends. Yet know this: my master, all-powerful God, is gathering armies of plague in his clouds on our behalf. They will strike your children, still unborn and not yet conceived, because you raise your servants’ hands against my head and threaten the glory of my precious crown. Tell Bolingbroke—I think that’s him standing over there—that every step he takes on my land is dangerous treason. He has come to open the bloody red will and testament of war. But before the crown he’s after can rest in peace, ten thousand bloody heads of mothers’ sons will disfigure the flower of England’s face. They will change her pale, maidenly peace into scarlet rage, and wet her pastures’ grass with loyal English blood.

NORTHUMBERLAND. May the King of Heaven forbid that our lord the King should be attacked like this by civil war’s savage weapons! Your three-times-noble cousin, Harry Bolingbroke, humbly kisses your hand. He swears by the honorable tomb that stands over your royal grandfather’s bones. He swears by the royal blood of both of you, streams that flow from one most gracious source. He swears by the buried hand of warlike Gaunt, and by his own worth and honor, which includes everything that can be sworn or said. He swears that his coming here has no other purpose than to claim his inherited rights. He wants to beg on his knees for his immediate freedom from banishment. Once your royal side grants that, he will leave his shining armor to rust and his armored horses to their stables. He will devote his heart to faithful service of your Majesty. He swears this as a prince and an honest man, and as a gentleman, I believe him.

KING RICHARD. Northumberland, tell him that this is the King’s answer. His noble cousin is very welcome here, and all his reasonable demands will be met without objection. Use all the gracious words you have to give him my kind regards.
[Northumberland goes back to Bolingbroke.]
[To Aumerle.] We’re lowering ourselves, cousin, aren’t we, by looking so humble and speaking so kindly? Shall we call Northumberland back, send defiance to the traitor, and so die?
AUMERLE. No, my good lord. Let’s fight with gentle words until time brings us friends, and those friends bring their helpful swords.

KING RICHARD. O God, O God! This tongue of mine passed the sentence of terrible banishment on that proud man. Must it now take it back with soothing words? Oh, I wish I were as great as my grief, or smaller than my title! Or I wish I could forget what I have been, or not remember what I must be now! Are you swelling, proud heart? I’ll give you room to beat, since my enemies have room to beat both you and me.
AUMERLE. Northumberland is coming back from Bolingbroke.

KING RICHARD. What must the King do now? Must he submit? The King will do it. Must he be deposed? The King will be satisfied. Must he lose the name of King? In God’s name, let it go. I’ll trade my jewels for a set of prayer beads and my magnificent palace for a hermit’s hut. I’ll trade my fine clothes for a beggar’s gown and my engraved goblets for a wooden bowl. I’ll trade my scepter for a pilgrim’s walking stick, my subjects for a pair of carved saints, and my large kingdom for a little grave. A little, little grave, an obscure grave. Or I’ll be buried in the King’s highway, some busy road where my subjects’ feet can trample on their sovereign’s head every hour. They tread on my heart now while I’m alive, so once I’m buried, why not on my head? Aumerle, you’re crying, my tender-hearted cousin! We’ll make foul weather with our scorned tears. Our sighs and tears will flatten the summer wheat and cause a famine in this rebellious land. Or shall we play games with our sorrows and make up some pretty contest of shedding tears? For example, we could keep dropping them on one spot until they have worn a pair of graves for us in the earth. Then, laid in them, our epitaph would read: here lie two kinsmen who dug their graves with weeping eyes. Wouldn’t this misery work well? Well, well, I see I’m talking nonsense, and you’re laughing at me. Most mighty prince, my Lord Northumberland, what does King Bolingbroke say? Will his Majesty give Richard permission to live until Richard dies? You bow, and that means Bolingbroke says yes.
NORTHUMBERLAND. My lord, he’s waiting in the lower courtyard to speak with you. Would you please come down?

KING RICHARD. Down, down I come, like shining Phaëthon, who couldn’t control the unruly horses of the sun’s chariot. In the base court? The base court, where kings become base by coming when traitors call and showing them favor. In the base court? Come down? Down, court! Down, king! Night owls are shrieking where soaring larks should sing.
[They exit from the walls above.]
BOLINGBROKE. What does his Majesty say?
NORTHUMBERLAND. Sorrow and grief make him talk foolishly, like a man out of his mind. Still, he’s coming.
[King Richard and his attendants enter.]
BOLINGBROKE. Everyone stand back and show proper respect to his Majesty. [He kneels.] My gracious lord.

KING RICHARD. Fair cousin, you lower your princely knee and make the lowly ground proud by kissing it. I would rather my heart could feel your love than have my displeased eyes watch your courtesy. Get up, cousin, get up. I know your heart is up—at least this high—even though your knee is low.
BOLINGBROKE. My gracious lord, I’ve come only for what is mine.
KING RICHARD. What is yours is yours, and I am yours, and everything is.
BOLINGBROKE. Let me have only as much, my most respected lord, as my true service earns of your love.

KING RICHARD. You deserve it well. Those who know the strongest and surest way to get things deserve to have them. Uncle, give me your hands. No, dry your eyes. Tears show love, but they offer no cure. Cousin, I’m too young to be your father, though you’re old enough to be my heir. Whatever you want, I’ll give, and willingly too, because we must do what force makes us do. Are we heading for London, cousin? Is that it?
BOLINGBROKE. Yes, my good lord.
KING RICHARD. Then I can’t say no.
[Flourish. They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 4 — Langley. The Duke of York’s garden
paragraphs: [The Queen and two Ladies enter.]
QUEEN. What game can we come up with here in this garden to drive away the heavy weight of worry?
LADY. Madam, we’ll play lawn bowling.
QUEEN. That will make me think the world is full of bumps that knock the ball off course, and that my luck is rolling the wrong way.
LADY. Madam, we’ll dance.
QUEEN. My legs can’t keep time with pleasure when my poor heart can’t keep any limit to its grief. So no dancing, girl. Some other game.
LADY. Madam, we’ll tell stories.
QUEEN. Sad ones or happy ones?
LADY. Either, madam.

QUEEN. Neither, girl. If they’re happy, since I have no happiness at all, they’ll only remind me more of my sorrow. If they’re sad, since I’m already full of grief, they’ll add more sorrow to my lack of joy. There’s no need to repeat the grief I already have, and it does no good to complain about the joy I lack.
LADY. Madam, I’ll sing.
QUEEN. It’s good that you have reason to sing. But you would please me more if you would cry.
LADY. I could cry, madam, if it would do you any good.

QUEEN. And I could sing, if crying did me any good, and I would never need to borrow a single tear from you. But wait, here come the gardeners. Let’s step into the shade of these trees. I’ll bet my misery against a row of pins that they’ll talk about politics. Everyone does when a change is coming. Sorrow is always announced by sorrow.
[The Queen and her Ladies step aside.]
[A Gardener and two Servants enter.]

GARDENER. You, go tie up those dangling young apricots. Like unruly children, they make their father bend over under the burden of their wasteful weight. Give some support to the bending branches. You, go and act like an executioner. Cut off the heads of the shoots that grow too fast and stand too tall in our commonwealth. Everything must be even in our government. While you two do that, I’ll go and root out the harmful weeds that uselessly suck the soil’s richness away from the healthy flowers.

SERVANT. Why should we, inside the boundary of a fence, keep law and order and proper proportion, showing in miniature what a well-run state looks like? Our sea-walled garden, the whole country, is full of weeds. Her loveliest flowers are choked. Her fruit trees are all unpruned and her hedges ruined. Her flowerbeds are in disorder, and her healthy herbs are swarming with caterpillars.

GARDENER. Be quiet. The man who allowed this disordered spring has now met his own autumn, when the leaves fall. The weeds that his broad, spreading leaves sheltered, which seemed to hold him up while they were eating him, have been pulled up, root and all, by Bolingbroke. I mean the Earl of Wiltshire, Bushy and Green.
SERVANT. What, are they dead?

GARDENER. They are. And Bolingbroke has captured the wasteful King. Oh, what a pity it is that he didn’t trim and tend his land the way we tend this garden! At the right time of year we cut into the bark, the skin of our fruit trees. Otherwise, swollen with too much sap and blood, the tree would ruin itself with its own richness. If he had done that to great men who were growing too powerful, they might have lived to bear the fruits of loyalty, and he might have lived to taste them. We cut away surplus branches so that the fruit-bearing boughs can live. If he had done that, he would still be wearing the crown, which his wasted, idle hours have thrown down completely.
SERVANT. What, do you think the King will be deposed?
GARDENER. He’s already brought low, and it’s likely he’ll be deposed. Letters came last night to a close friend of the good Duke of York’s. They carry dark news.
QUEEN. Oh, I’m being crushed to death because I can’t speak!
[She comes forward.]

You, made in old Adam’s image and set to tend this garden, how dare your harsh, rough tongue spread this unpleasant news? What Eve, what serpent, has tempted you to cause a second fall of cursed mankind? Why do you say King Richard is deposed? Do you dare, you thing hardly better than dirt, to predict his downfall? Tell me where, when and how you came by this bad news. Speak, you wretch!

GARDENER. Forgive me, madam. I take little joy in telling this news, but what I say is true. King Richard is in Bolingbroke’s powerful grip. Their fortunes have both been weighed on the scales. In your husband’s pan there is nothing but himself and a few vanities that make him light. But on great Bolingbroke’s side, besides himself, are all the English lords. With that advantage he outweighs King Richard. Hurry to London, and you’ll find it’s true. I’m saying no more than everyone already knows.

QUEEN. Quick-footed bad luck, so light on your feet, isn’t this message meant for me? And am I the last to know it? Oh, you think you’ll serve me last so that I keep your sorrow in my heart the longest. Come, ladies, let’s go to London to meet London’s king in his misery. What, was I born for this, so that my sad face would decorate great Bolingbroke’s victory parade? Gardener, for telling me this miserable news, I pray to God the plants you graft never grow!
[The Queen and her ladies exit.]

GARDENER. Poor Queen, if it would keep your situation from getting worse, I’d gladly let your curse fall on my skill. She dropped a tear here. Right in this spot I’ll plant a bed of rue, the bitter herb of grace. Rue, which stands for pity, will soon grow here in memory of a weeping queen.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — Westminster Hall
paragraphs: [The bishops sit on the right side of the throne, the noble lords on the left, and the Commons below. Bolingbroke, Aumerle, Surrey, Northumberland, Harry Percy, Fitzwater, another Lord, the Bishop of Carlisle, the Abbot of Westminster and attendants enter.]
BOLINGBROKE. Bring in Bagot.
[Officers enter with Bagot.]
Now, Bagot, speak your mind freely. Tell us what you know about noble Gloucester’s death: who arranged it with the King, and who carried out the bloody job of killing him before his time.
BAGOT. Then bring Lord Aumerle here to face me.
BOLINGBROKE. Cousin, step forward and look at that man.

BAGOT. My Lord Aumerle, I know your bold tongue is too proud to take back anything it has once said. In that deadly time when Gloucester’s death was being plotted, I heard you say, “Isn’t my arm long enough to reach from the peaceful English court all the way to Calais, to my uncle’s head?” In a lot of other talk at that same time, I heard you say you would rather turn down an offer of a hundred thousand crowns than see Bolingbroke come back to England. You added how blessed this country would be if your cousin died.

AUMERLE. Princes and noble lords, what answer should I give this lowborn man? Should I disgrace my noble birth so much as to fight him as an equal? Either I must, or let my honor be stained by the accusation from his slanderous lips. There is my glove, the hand-signed death warrant that marks you for hell. I say you’re lying. I will prove what you said is false with your own heart’s blood, though it’s far too lowly to stain the steel of my knightly sword.
BOLINGBROKE. Bagot, stop. You will not pick it up.
AUMERLE. With one exception, I wish the man who has provoked me like this were the highest-ranking person in this whole assembly.

FITZWATER. If your courage insists on fighting someone of equal rank, there is my glove, Aumerle, thrown down to match yours. By that bright sun that shows me where you stand, I heard you say, and you said it boastfully, that you caused noble Gloucester’s death. If you deny it twenty times, you’re lying! And I will drive your lie back into your heart, where it was made, with the point of my rapier.
AUMERLE. You coward, you wouldn’t dare live to see that day.
FITZWATER. Now, by my soul, I wish it were this very hour.
AUMERLE. Fitzwater, you’re damned to hell for this.

HARRY PERCY. Aumerle, you’re lying. His honor is as true in this accusation as you are false. To show that you are, I throw down my glove there. I’ll prove it on you until your last breath of life. Pick it up if you dare.
AUMERLE. And if I don’t, may my hands rot off and never again swing vengeful steel over my enemy’s shining helmet!

ANOTHER LORD. I load the earth with the same challenge, you lying Aumerle. I’ll spur you on with as many accusations of lying as can be shouted into your treacherous ear from sunrise to sunset. There is the pledge of my honor. Take it up for a trial by combat if you dare.
AUMERLE. Who else challenges me? By heaven, I’ll take on all of you. I have a thousand spirits in one chest to answer twenty thousand men like you.
SURREY. My Lord Fitzwater, I remember very well the exact time when you and Aumerle talked.
FITZWATER. That’s quite true. You were there then, and you can testify with me that this is true.
SURREY. It’s as false, by heaven, as heaven itself is true.
FITZWATER. Surrey, you’re lying.

SURREY. You dishonorable boy! That lie will lie so heavy on my sword that it will deliver vengeance and revenge until you, the liar, and your lie both lie in the ground as quiet as your father’s skull. To prove it, there is the pledge of my honor. Take it up for a trial by combat if you dare.

FITZWATER. How foolishly you spur a horse that’s already eager to run! If I dare eat, or drink, or breathe, or live, I dare meet Surrey in a wilderness and spit on him while I say he lies, and lies, and lies. There is my pledge to bind you to my harsh punishment. As surely as I hope to prosper in this new order, Aumerle is guilty of what I truly accuse him of. Besides, I heard the banished Norfolk say that you, Aumerle, sent two of your men to kill the noble duke at Calais.
AUMERLE. Some honest Christian lend me a glove. I throw this down to say Norfolk lies, if he can be called back from exile to defend his honor.

BOLINGBROKE. All these disputes will stay on hold, pledges and all, until Norfolk is called back. And called back he will be. Even though he’s my enemy, he’ll be restored to all his lands and estates. When he returns, we will make him face Aumerle in a trial by combat.

CARLISLE. That honorable day will never be seen. Many times the banished Norfolk fought for Jesus Christ on glorious Christian battlefields. He flew the banner of the Christian cross against black pagans, Turks and Saracens. Then, worn out by the labors of war, he retired to Italy. There, in Venice, he gave his body to that pleasant country’s earth, and his pure soul to his captain, Christ, under whose flag he had fought so long.
BOLINGBROKE. What, Bishop, is Norfolk dead?
CARLISLE. As surely as I’m alive, my lord.

BOLINGBROKE. May sweet peace guide his sweet soul to the bosom of good old Abraham! Lords who have made these accusations, your disputes will all stay on hold, pledges and all, until we set dates for your trials.
[York enters with attendants.]

YORK. Great Duke of Lancaster, I come to you from Richard, whose feathers have been plucked. With a willing heart he adopts you as his heir. He hands his high scepter over into the possession of your royal hand. Climb up to his throne, which he is now stepping down from. And long live Henry, the fourth king of that name!
BOLINGBROKE. In God’s name, I’ll climb up to the royal throne.

CARLISLE. God forbid it! I may be the lowest-ranking person speaking in this royal company, but it suits me best to speak the truth. I wish to God anyone in this noble company were noble enough to be a fair judge of noble Richard! Then true nobility would teach him to hold back from such a foul wrong. What subject can pass sentence on his king? And who sits here who isn’t Richard’s subject? Even thieves aren’t judged unless they’re present to hear it, though their guilt is obvious. And should the image of God’s majesty—his captain, steward and chosen deputy, anointed, crowned and established for many years—be judged by the voices of subjects and inferiors, without even being present himself? Oh, God forbid that in a Christian country refined souls should commit such a hateful, black and disgusting act! I speak to subjects, and I, a subject, speak this boldly for my king, stirred up by God. My Lord of Hereford here, whom you call king, is a foul traitor to proud Hereford’s king. If you crown him, let me prophesy this. The blood of English people will fertilize the ground, and future generations will groan for this foul act. Peace will go to sleep among Turks and unbelievers. Here, in this home of peace, chaotic wars will make kin destroy kin and countryman destroy countryman. Disorder, horror, fear and rebellion will live here, and this land will be called the field of Golgotha, the place of dead men’s skulls. Oh, if you raise this royal house against that royal house, it will prove the most miserable division that ever fell on this cursed earth. Prevent it, resist it, don’t let it happen. Otherwise your children and your children’s children will cry out against you, “woe!”

NORTHUMBERLAND. You’ve argued well, sir, and for your trouble, we arrest you here for high treason. My Lord of Westminster, it’s your job to keep him safely locked up until his trial. My lords, will you grant the request of the Commons?
BOLINGBROKE. Bring Richard here so he can surrender in public view. That way we can proceed without arousing suspicion.
YORK. I’ll escort him.
[He exits.]
BOLINGBROKE. Lords, you who are under arrest here, arrange for people to guarantee you’ll appear on your trial days. We owe little to your love, and we expected little help from your hands.
[York enters with King Richard and officers carrying the crown and other royal emblems.]

KING RICHARD. Oh, why am I summoned to a king before I’ve shaken off the royal thoughts I ruled with? I’ve barely learned yet how to wheedle, flatter, bow and bend my knee. Give sorrow some time to teach me this submission. Still, I remember these men’s faces well. Weren’t they mine? Didn’t they once shout “All hail!” to me? Judas did the same to Christ. But Christ found loyalty in all of his twelve except one. I, out of twelve thousand, found none. God save the King! Will no one say “Amen”? Do I have to be both the priest and the clerk who answers him? Well then, amen. God save the King, even though I’m not him. And yet amen, if heaven thinks he is me. What service have I been brought here to do?
YORK. To do, of your own free will, the task that your weary majesty offered to do: to resign your power and crown to Henry Bolingbroke.

KING RICHARD. Give me the crown. Here, cousin, take hold of the crown. Here, cousin, my hand on this side and yours on that side. Now this golden crown is like a deep well that has two buckets, each one filling the other in turn. The emptier one always dances up in the air. The other is down below, unseen and full of water. I am that bucket down below, full of tears, drinking my griefs while you rise up high.
BOLINGBROKE. I thought you were willing to resign.
KING RICHARD. I’m willing to give up my crown, but my griefs are still mine. You can strip away my glories and my power, but not my griefs. I am still king of those.
BOLINGBROKE. Along with your crown you give me part of your worries.

KING RICHARD. Your worries rising up don’t take my worries down. My worry is the loss of my responsibility, caused by my old neglect. Your worry is the gain of responsibility, won by your new efforts. The cares I hand over I still keep, even though I give them away. They attend the crown, yet they still stay with me.
BOLINGBROKE. Are you content to resign the crown?

KING RICHARD. Yes, no; no, yes. I must be nothing, so I can’t say “no,” because I resign to you. Now watch how I will unmake myself. I take this heavy weight off my head and this clumsy scepter from my hand. I take the pride of royal power out of my heart. With my own tears I wash away the holy oil that anointed me. With my own hands I give away my crown. With my own tongue I deny my sacred position. With my own breath I release everyone from their oaths of loyalty. I renounce all pomp and majesty. I give up my manors, rents and revenues. I revoke my acts, decrees and laws. May God pardon all the oaths that are broken to me. May God keep unbroken all the vows that are made to you. May he make me, who has nothing, grieved by nothing. And may you, who have gained everything, be pleased with everything. Long may you live to sit on Richard’s throne, and may Richard soon lie in a grave in the earth! Unkinged Richard says, God save King Henry, and send him many years of sunny days! What else is left?

NORTHUMBERLAND. [Offering a paper.] Nothing more, except that you read out these accusations and these serious crimes committed by you and your followers against the welfare and profit of this country. That way, by your confessing them, people’s souls may judge that you deserved to be deposed.

KING RICHARD. Must I do that? And must I unravel my tangled-up follies? Noble Northumberland, if your own crimes were written down, wouldn’t you be ashamed to read them out as a lecture in front of such a fine crowd? If you did, you would find one hateful item there. It would record the deposing of a king and the breaking of a sacred oath, marked with a stain and damned in heaven’s book. No, all of you who stand and stare at me while my misery torments me like a baited bear—though some of you wash your hands like Pilate and show pity on the outside—you Pilates have still handed me over to my bitter cross, and no water can wash away your sin.
NORTHUMBERLAND. My lord, hurry up. Read through these charges.

KING RICHARD. My eyes are full of tears. I can’t see. And yet the salt water doesn’t blind them so much that they can’t see a pack of traitors here. No, if I turn my eyes on myself, I find I’m a traitor along with the rest. Here I have given my soul’s consent to strip the splendid body of a king. I’ve made glory lowly and sovereignty a slave. I’ve made proud majesty a subject and royal state a peasant.
NORTHUMBERLAND. My lord—

KING RICHARD. I’m no lord of yours, you arrogant, insulting man, and no man’s lord at all! I have no name and no title. No, not even the name I was given at the baptismal font, because it’s been taken from me. Oh, what a heavy day! I have lived through so many winters, and now I don’t know what name to call myself. Oh, if only I were a mock king made of snow, standing before the sun of Bolingbroke, so I could melt myself away in drops of water! Good king, great king, and yet not greatly good, if my word is still worth anything in England, let it order a mirror brought here right away. Then it can show me what kind of face I have, now that my face is bankrupt of its majesty.
BOLINGBROKE. Some of you, go and get a mirror.
[An attendant exits.]
NORTHUMBERLAND. Read this paper while the mirror is coming.
KING RICHARD. Devil, you torment me before I even get to hell!
BOLINGBROKE. Don’t press it any more, my Lord Northumberland.
NORTHUMBERLAND. Then the Commons won’t be satisfied.
KING RICHARD. They will be satisfied. I’ll read plenty when I see the real book where all my sins are written, and that book is me.
[The attendant enters again with a mirror.]

Give me that mirror, and I will read myself in it. No deeper wrinkles yet? Has sorrow struck so many blows on this face of mine and left no deeper wounds? Oh, flattering mirror, you deceive me, just like my followers did when times were good. Was this the face that kept ten thousand men under its household roof every day? Was this the face that, like the sun, made people who looked at it blink? Is this the face that put a good face on so many follies, and was finally outfaced by Bolingbroke? A brittle glory shines in this face. And the face is as brittle as the glory!
[He smashes the mirror on the ground.]
There it is, cracked into a hundred splinters. Note, silent king, the moral of this game: see how quickly my sorrow has destroyed my face.
BOLINGBROKE. It was only the shadow of your sorrow that destroyed the shadow of your face.

KING RICHARD. Say that again. The shadow of my sorrow? Ha, let me think. That’s very true: my grief lies entirely inside me. These outward ways of mourning are only shadows of the unseen grief that swells silently in my tortured soul. That is where the real substance lies. And I thank you, king, for your great generosity. You not only give me reason to weep, but also teach me how to mourn that reason. I’ll beg one favor, and then I’ll go and trouble you no more. Will I get it?
BOLINGBROKE. Name it, fair cousin.

KING RICHARD. “Fair cousin”? Why, I am greater than a king. When I was a king, my flatterers were only my subjects. Now that I am a subject, I have a king here as my flatterer. Being so great, I have no need to beg.
BOLINGBROKE. Ask anyway.
KING RICHARD. And will I get what I ask for?
BOLINGBROKE. You will.
KING RICHARD. Then give me permission to go.
BOLINGBROKE. Where to?
KING RICHARD. Wherever you like, as long as I’m out of your sight.
BOLINGBROKE. Some of you, go and convey him to the Tower.
KING RICHARD. Oh, good! “Convey”? You’re all conveyors, thieves, the lot of you, who rise so nimbly by a true king’s fall.
[King Richard and the Guard exit.]
BOLINGBROKE. Next Wednesday we formally set our coronation. Lords, prepare yourselves.
[Everyone exits except the Bishop of Carlisle, the Abbot of Westminster and Aumerle.]
ABBOT. We have watched a woeful spectacle here.
CARLISLE. The real woe is still to come. Children not yet born will feel this day as sharply as a thorn.
AUMERLE. You holy clergymen, is there no plot to rid the kingdom of this deadly stain?

ABBOT. My lord, before I speak my mind freely on this, you must take the sacrament. You must swear not only to keep my intentions buried, but also to carry out whatever I happen to devise. I see your brows are full of discontent, your hearts full of sorrow, and your eyes full of tears. Come home with me for supper. I will lay out a plot that will bring us all a happy day.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — London. A street leading to the Tower
paragraphs: [The Queen and her ladies enter.]

QUEEN. The King will come this way. This is the road to the tower Julius Caesar built for evil ends. Proud Bolingbroke has doomed my condemned husband to be a prisoner in its stony heart. Let’s rest here, if this rebellious earth has any rest to offer its true king’s queen.
[King Richard and the Guard enter.]

But quiet, look—or rather, don’t look—at my fair rose withering. Yet look up, look at him, so that you may melt into dew out of pity and wash him fresh again with tears of true love. Ah, you are like the ruined site where old Troy once stood. You are the very outline of honor, King Richard’s tomb, and not King Richard himself! You most beautiful inn, why should ugly grief lodge in you, when triumph has become a guest at a common alehouse?

KING RICHARD. Don’t join forces with grief, fair woman, don’t, or you’ll bring my end too suddenly. Learn, good soul, to think of our former greatness as a happy dream. Now that we’ve woken from it, the truth of what we are shows us only this. I am sworn brother, sweetheart, to grim Necessity, and he and I will stay allies until death. Hurry to France and shut yourself away in some convent. Our holy lives must win a crown in the next world, since our unholy hours here have thrown this one down.

QUEEN. What, is my Richard transformed and weakened in both body and mind? Has Bolingbroke deposed your intellect too? Has he been inside your heart? A dying lion thrusts out his paw and wounds the earth, if nothing else, in rage at being overpowered. And will you, like a schoolboy, take your punishment meekly? Will you kiss the rod and fawn on cruelty with low humility, when you are a lion and the king of beasts?

KING RICHARD. A king of beasts, indeed! If they had been anything but beasts, I would still be a happy king of men. Good former queen, get ready to leave for France. Think of me as dead, and that here, as if at my deathbed, you are taking your last leave of me while I live. On long winter nights, sit by the fire with good old people and let them tell you stories of sad ages that happened long ago. Before you say good night, pay them back for their sad stories. Tell them the pitiful tale of me, and send your listeners weeping to their beds. Because even the senseless logs will feel for the heavy sound of your moving voice. Out of compassion they will weep the fire out. Some will mourn in ashes, some in coal-black, for the deposing of a rightful king.
[Northumberland enters with attendants.]

NORTHUMBERLAND. My lord, Bolingbroke has changed his mind. You must go to Pomfret, not to the Tower. And, madam, arrangements have been made for you: you must leave for France with all possible speed.

KING RICHARD. Northumberland, you are the ladder that climbing Bolingbroke uses to mount my throne. Not many hours will pass before foul sin comes to a head like a boil and bursts into corruption. You will think that even if he divides the kingdom and gives you half, it is too little for helping him to all of it. And he will think that you, who know how to plant illegitimate kings, will find another way. With the slightest push, you’ll know how to pull him headlong off the throne he stole. The love of wicked men turns to fear, that fear turns to hate, and hate brings one or both of them to deserved danger and well-earned death.
NORTHUMBERLAND. Let my guilt be on my head, and that’s the end of it. Say goodbye and separate, because you must part right now.

KING RICHARD. Divorced twice over! Wicked men, you violate a double marriage: the one between my crown and me, and the one between me and my wedded wife. Let me unkiss the vow between you and me. And yet no, because it was sealed with a kiss. Part us, Northumberland. I go north, where shivering cold and sickness waste the land away. My wife goes to France. She set out from there in splendor and came here dressed up like sweet May, and now she is sent back like Hallowmas in dark November, or the shortest day of the year.
QUEEN. Must we be separated? Must we part?
KING RICHARD. Yes, hand from hand, my love, and heart from heart.
QUEEN. Banish us both, and send the King with me.
NORTHUMBERLAND. That would be loving, but not very wise politics.
QUEEN. Then wherever he goes, let me go there too.

KING RICHARD. That way two people weeping together make only one sorrow. You weep for me in France, and I’ll weep for you here. Better to be far apart than near each other and never be any nearer. Go, and measure your journey with sighs, and I’ll measure mine with groans.
QUEEN. Then the longer journey will have the longer moans.

KING RICHARD. I’ll groan twice with every step, since my road is short, and stretch the way out with a heavy heart. Come, come, let’s be quick in courting sorrow, since once we are married to it, grief lasts so long. One kiss will seal our mouths, and we’ll part without words. This is how I give you my heart, and this is how I take yours.
[They kiss.]
QUEEN. Give me my own heart back. It would be wrong of me to keep your heart and kill it with grief.
[They kiss again.]
There, now I have my own heart back. Go, so that I can try to kill it with a groan.
KING RICHARD. We make sorrow playful with this foolish delay. Once more, goodbye. Let sorrow say the rest.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — The same. A room in the Duke of York’s palace
paragraphs: [York and his Duchess enter.]
DUCHESS. My lord, you said you would tell me the rest of the story of our two cousins arriving in London, when weeping made you break it off.
YORK. Where did I stop?
DUCHESS. At that sad point, my lord, where rough, unruly hands threw dust and garbage on King Richard’s head from the tops of windows.

YORK. Then, as I said, the Duke, great Bolingbroke, was mounted on a hot and fiery horse, which seemed to know its ambitious rider. He kept on his way at a slow but stately pace, while every voice shouted, “God save you, Bolingbroke!” You would have thought the very windows were speaking. So many eager looks from young and old darted their longing eyes out through the casements onto his face. It was as if all the walls hung with painted cloths had said at once, “Jesus preserve you! Welcome, Bolingbroke!” Meanwhile he kept turning from one side to the other, bareheaded, bowing lower than his proud horse’s neck. He spoke to them like this: “I thank you, countrymen.” And he kept doing that as he passed along.
DUCHESS. Alas, poor Richard! Where was he riding all this time?

YORK. In a theater, after a popular actor leaves the stage, people’s eyes turn lazily to the one who enters next, thinking his chatter will be boring. In just that way, or with much more contempt, men’s eyes scowled at gentle Richard. No one shouted “God save him!” No joyful voice welcomed him home. Instead, dust was thrown on his sacred head. He shook it off with such gentle sorrow, his face still struggling between tears and smiles, the signs of his grief and his patience. If God had not hardened men’s hearts for some powerful purpose, they would have had to melt. Even barbarism itself would have pitied him. But heaven has a hand in these events, and we submit calmly to its high will. We are now Bolingbroke’s sworn subjects, and I accept his rank and honor forever.
[Aumerle enters.]
DUCHESS. Here comes my son Aumerle.

YORK. He used to be Aumerle. But he has lost that title for being Richard’s friend, and, madam, you must call him Rutland now. I have pledged myself in Parliament as guarantee of his loyalty and lasting allegiance to the newly made king.
DUCHESS. Welcome, my son. Who are the violets now, the new favorites who scatter themselves over the green lap of this new spring?
AUMERLE. Madam, I don’t know, and I don’t much care. God knows I would just as soon be none of them as one of them.
YORK. Well, behave yourself in this new springtime, or you’ll be cut down before you come into flower. What news from Oxford? Are those jousts and celebrations still going ahead?
AUMERLE. As far as I know, my lord, they are.
YORK. You’ll be there, I know.
AUMERLE. Unless God prevents it, I intend to be.
YORK. What seal is that hanging outside your shirt? What, you look pale? Let me see the document.
AUMERLE. My lord, it’s nothing.
YORK. Then it doesn’t matter who sees it. I’ll have my answer. Let me see the document.
AUMERLE. I beg your Grace to excuse me. It’s a matter of little importance, which for certain reasons I would rather nobody saw.
YORK. And for certain reasons, sir, I intend to see it. I fear, I fear—
DUCHESS. What are you afraid of? It’s nothing but some IOU he has signed for fancy clothes for the day of the celebrations.
YORK. A bond to himself? What would he be doing with a bond that he holds against himself? Wife, you’re a fool. Boy, let me see the document.
AUMERLE. I beg you, excuse me. I can’t show it.
YORK. I’ll have my answer. Let me see it, I tell you.
[He snatches it and reads it.]
Treason, foul treason! Villain! Traitor! Slave!
DUCHESS. What’s the matter, my lord?
YORK. Hey! Who’s in there?
[A Servant enters.]
Saddle my horse. God have mercy, what treachery is this!
DUCHESS. Why, what is it, my lord?
YORK. Give me my boots, I tell you. Saddle my horse. Now, by my honor, by my life, by my faith, I will denounce the villain.
[The Servant exits.]
DUCHESS. What’s the matter?
YORK. Quiet, foolish woman.
DUCHESS. I won’t be quiet. What’s the matter, Aumerle?
AUMERLE. Good mother, calm down. It’s nothing more than my poor life will have to pay for.
DUCHESS. Your life pay for it?
YORK. Bring me my boots. I’m going to the King.
[The Servant enters again with boots.]
DUCHESS. Hit him, Aumerle! Poor boy, you’re stunned.
[To the Servant.]
Get out, villain! Never come into my sight again.
[The Servant exits.]
YORK. Give me my boots, I tell you.

DUCHESS. Why, York, what are you going to do? Won’t you hide the wrongdoing of your own flesh and blood? Do we have any more sons? Are we likely to have any? Isn’t my child-bearing time long since swallowed up by age? And will you snatch my fair son away from me in my old age, and rob me of the name of happy mother? Isn’t he like you? Isn’t he your own?

YORK. You foolish, mad woman, would you hide this dark conspiracy? A dozen of them here have taken the sacrament and signed their names to each other’s copies. They have sworn to kill the King at Oxford.
DUCHESS. He won’t be one of them. We’ll keep him here. Then what does it have to do with him?
YORK. Get away, foolish woman! If he were my son twenty times over, I would denounce him.

DUCHESS. If you had groaned in labor for him as I did, you would be more merciful. But now I know what you’re thinking. You suspect that I have been unfaithful to your bed, and that he is a bastard, not your son. Sweet York, sweet husband, don’t think that way. He is as like you as a man can be. He is not like me, or any of my family, and yet I love him.
YORK. Get out of my way, unruly woman!
[He exits.]

DUCHESS. After him, Aumerle! Get on his horse! Ride hard, and get to the King before he does. Beg for your pardon before he accuses you. I won’t be far behind. Though I am old, I’m sure I can ride as fast as York. And I will never rise up from the ground until Bolingbroke has pardoned you. Go, be gone!
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 3 — Windsor. A room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Bolingbroke enters as King, with Harry Percy and other Lords.]

KING HENRY. Can no one tell me anything about my wasteful son? It’s been a full three months since I last saw him. If any plague hangs over us, it’s him. I wish to God, my lords, that he could be found. Ask around London, among the taverns there. They say he goes there every day with loose, unruly companions. They say they are the kind who lurk in narrow alleys, beat up our watchmen and rob travelers. Meanwhile he, that spoiled and unmanly boy, makes it a point of honor to support such a dissolute gang.
PERCY. My lord, about two days ago I saw the Prince and told him about the tournament being held at Oxford.
KING HENRY. And what did the fine young gentleman say?

PERCY. His answer was that he would go to the brothels and pull a glove off the commonest whore. He would wear it as a lady’s token, and with that he would knock the strongest challenger off his horse.
KING HENRY. As dissolute as he is reckless! Yet through both I see some sparks of better hope, which older years may happily bring out. But who is coming here?
[Aumerle enters.]
AUMERLE. Where is the King?
KING HENRY. What does our cousin mean, staring and looking so wild?
AUMERLE. God save your Grace! I beg your majesty to let me speak with your Grace alone.
KING HENRY. Withdraw, all of you, and leave us here alone.
[Harry Percy and the Lords exit.]
What’s the matter with our cousin now?
AUMERLE. [He kneels.] May my knees grow into the ground forever, and my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth, unless I have a pardon before I get up or speak.
KING HENRY. Was this offense only planned, or actually committed? If it was only planned, however wicked it may be, I pardon you, to win your love from now on.
AUMERLE. Then allow me to lock the door, so that no one comes in until I’ve finished my story.
KING HENRY. Do as you wish.
[Aumerle locks the door.]
YORK. [From offstage.] My lord, beware! Look out for yourself! You have a traitor there in your presence.
KING HENRY. [Drawing his sword.] Villain, I’ll make you harmless.
AUMERLE. Hold back your vengeful hand. You have no reason to be afraid.
YORK. [From offstage.] Open the door, you careless, reckless king! Must I speak treason to your face out of love for you? Open the door, or I’ll break it down.
[King Henry unlocks the door, and afterward locks it again.]
[York enters.]
KING HENRY. What is the matter, uncle? Speak! Catch your breath. Tell us how close the danger is, so that we can arm ourselves to meet it.
YORK. Read this document, and you will learn the treason that I am too out of breath to explain.
AUMERLE. As you read it, remember the promise you made. I repent. Don’t read my name there. My heart is not in league with my hand.

YORK. It was, villain, before your hand signed it. I tore this from the traitor’s chest, king. Fear, not love, is what makes him repent. Don’t pity him, or your pity may turn out to be a snake that will sting you to the heart.

KING HENRY. Oh, wicked, powerful and bold conspiracy! Oh, loyal father of a treacherous son! You pure, spotless, silver fountain! From you this stream has run its course through muddy channels and dirtied itself. Your overflowing goodness turns into his badness. And your abundant goodness will excuse this deadly stain in your wayward son.

YORK. That way my own goodness would become the pimp that serves his wickedness. He would squander my honor to pay for his shame, the way wasteful sons blow the gold their penny-pinching fathers scraped together. My honor lives only if his dishonor dies. Otherwise my life will lie disgraced in his dishonor. If you let him live, you kill me. By giving him breath, you let the traitor live and put the loyal man to death.
DUCHESS. [From offstage.] Hello there, my lord! For God’s sake, let me in!
KING HENRY. Who is this shrill-voiced petitioner crying out so urgently?
DUCHESS. [From offstage.] It’s a woman, great king, and your aunt. It’s me. Speak to me, have pity on me, open the door! A beggar who has never begged before is begging you.
KING HENRY. Our play has changed from a serious drama into “The Beggar and the King.” My dangerous cousin, let your mother in. I know she’s come to plead for your foul sin.
[The Duchess enters.]

YORK. If you pardon whoever begs you, this forgiveness will only let more sins thrive. Cut off this infected limb, and the rest of the body stays healthy. Leave it alone, and it will ruin all the rest.
DUCHESS. Oh King, don’t believe this hard-hearted man. A man who doesn’t love his own flesh and blood can’t love anyone else.
YORK. You crazy woman, what are you doing here? Are your old breasts going to nurse another traitor?
DUCHESS. Sweet York, be patient. [She kneels.] Listen to me, gracious lord.
KING HENRY. Get up, good aunt.
DUCHESS. Not yet, I beg you. I will walk on my knees forever and never see a day the happy see, until you give me joy. Until you tell me to be joyful by pardoning Rutland, my sinful boy.
AUMERLE. I kneel too, joining my mother’s prayers.
[He kneels.]
YORK. And I bend my loyal knees against both of them.
[He kneels.]
May things go badly for you if you grant them any mercy!

DUCHESS. Is he pleading seriously? Look at his face. His eyes shed no tears, and his prayers are a joke. His words come from his mouth; ours come from our hearts. He prays weakly and wants to be refused. We pray with our hearts and souls and everything else. His tired knees would happily get up, I know. Ours will keep kneeling until they grow into the ground. His prayers are full of false hypocrisy; ours are full of true passion and deep honesty. Our prayers outpray his, so let them receive the mercy that true prayer deserves.
KING HENRY. Good aunt, stand up.

DUCHESS. No, don’t say “stand up.” Say “pardon” first, and after that “stand up.” If I were your nurse, teaching you to talk, “Pardon” would be the first word you ever said. I never longed to hear a word until now. Say “pardon,” king. Let pity teach you how. It’s a short word, but its sweetness is not short. No word is so fitting for a king’s mouth as “pardon.”
YORK. Say it in French, King: say “pardonne moy.”

DUCHESS. Are you teaching him to use pardon to destroy pardon? Ah, my sour husband, my hard-hearted lord, setting the word against itself! Say “pardon” the way it’s used in our country. We don’t understand this word-chopping French. Your eyes are starting to speak mercy, so put your tongue there too. Or plant your ear in your pitying heart. Then, hearing how our complaints and prayers pierce it, pity may move you to say “pardon.”
KING HENRY. Good aunt, stand up.
DUCHESS. I’m not asking to stand. Pardon is the only thing I’m asking for.
KING HENRY. I pardon him, just as I hope God will pardon me.
DUCHESS. Oh, what a happy gain from a kneeling knee! But I’m still sick with fear. Say it again. Saying “pardon” twice doesn’t mean two pardons. It makes one pardon stronger.
KING HENRY. I pardon him with all my heart.
DUCHESS. You are a god on earth.

KING HENRY. But as for our trusted brother-in-law and the Abbot, and the rest of that conspiring gang, destruction will hunt them down at once. Good uncle, help organize separate forces and send them to Oxford, or wherever these traitors are. I swear they won’t stay alive in this world. Once I know where they are, I’ll have them. Uncle, farewell. And cousin, goodbye. Your mother prayed well for you, so prove yourself loyal.
DUCHESS. Come, my old son. I pray to God he makes you new.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 4 — Another room in the Castle
paragraphs: [Exton and a Servant enter.]
EXTON. Didn’t you notice what the King said? “Do I have no friend who will rid me of this living fear?” Isn’t that how it went?
SERVANT. Those were his exact words.
EXTON. “Do I have no friend?” he said. He said it twice and pressed it twice in a row, didn’t he?
SERVANT. He did.

EXTON. And as he said it, he looked at me meaningfully, as if to say, “I wish you were the man who would separate this terror from my heart.” He meant the former king at Pomfret. Come on, let’s go. I am the King’s friend, and I will get rid of his enemy.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 5 — Pomfret. The dungeon of the Castle
paragraphs: [Richard enters.]

RICHARD. I have been working out how I could compare this prison where I live to the world. But the world is full of people, and here there is no creature but me, so I can’t do it. Still, I’ll hammer it out. I’ll make my brain the mother and my soul the father. These two will produce a family of thoughts that keep on breeding. These thoughts will populate this little world, with moods like the people of the real world, because no thought is ever satisfied. The better kind, such as thoughts about religion, are mixed with doubts. They set one scripture against another, like this: “Come, little children.” And then again: “It is as hard to come to heaven as for a camel to pass through the narrow gate of a needle’s eye.” Ambitious thoughts plot impossible wonders. They imagine how these feeble fingernails could tear a way out through the stony ribs of this hard world, my rough prison walls. And because they can’t, they die of their own pride. Contented thoughts comfort themselves that they aren’t the first slaves of fortune and won’t be the last. They are like simple beggars sitting in the stocks, who ease their shame by thinking that many have sat there and others will. In this thought they find a kind of relief, carrying their own bad luck on the backs of others who suffered the same before. So I play many people all by myself, and none of them is satisfied. Sometimes I’m a king. Then treasons make me wish I were a beggar, and so I am one. Then grinding poverty convinces me I was better off as a king. Then I’m king again. And soon after, I think that Bolingbroke has unkinged me, and right away I’m nothing. But whatever I am, neither I nor any other man who is merely human will be satisfied with anything until he finds rest in being nothing. Do I hear music? [Music plays.] Ha, ha! Keep time! How sour sweet music sounds when the beat is broken and the rhythm isn’t kept! It’s the same in the music of men’s lives. And here I have a fine enough ear to notice a broken beat on an out-of-tune string. But I didn’t have the ear to hear my true time broken, when my reign and my times fell out of harmony. I wasted time, and now time wastes me. Time has turned me into his clock that counts the minutes. My thoughts are minutes, and with sighs they tick on to my eyes, which are the clock face. My finger, like the hand of a clock, keeps pointing there as it wipes away tears. Now, sir, the sound that tells the hour is the loud groaning that strikes my heart, which is the bell. So sighs, tears and groans mark minutes, quarter hours and hours. But my time races on in Bolingbroke’s proud joy, while I stand here playing the fool, the little figure that strikes his clock’s bell. This music is driving me mad! Let it stop. It may have helped madmen recover their wits, but in me it seems it will drive a sane man mad. Still, bless the heart of whoever plays it for me, because it’s a sign of love. And love for Richard is a rare jewel in this world where everyone hates him.
[A Groom from the stables enters.]
GROOM. Greetings, royal Prince!

RICHARD. Thanks, noble peer. The cheaper of us two is still overpriced by ten groats. Who are you, and how did you get here? No one ever comes here except that gloomy dog who brings me food to keep my misery alive.

GROOM. I was a poor groom in your stables, king, when you were king. I’m traveling toward York, and after a lot of trouble I finally got permission to look at the face of my once-royal master. Oh, how it grieved my heart when I saw, in the London streets on that coronation day, Bolingbroke riding on roan Barbary! That’s the horse you rode so often, the horse I groomed so carefully.
RICHARD. He rode on Barbary? Tell me, kind friend, how did the horse carry him?
GROOM. As proudly as if he scorned the ground.

RICHARD. So proud that Bolingbroke was on his back! That nag has eaten bread from my royal hand. This hand made him proud by patting him. Couldn’t he have stumbled? Couldn’t he have fallen down, since pride must have a fall, and broken the neck of that proud man who stole his back? Forgive me, horse! Why do I scold you? You were created to be ruled by man and born to carry. I wasn’t made a horse, and yet I carry a load like a donkey. I’m spurred, rubbed raw and worn out by bouncing, prancing Bolingbroke.
[The Keeper enters with a dish.]
KEEPER. [To the Groom.] Fellow, make way. You can’t stay here any longer.
RICHARD. If you love me, it’s time you left.
GROOM. What my tongue doesn’t dare say, my heart will.
[He exits.]
KEEPER. My lord, would you like to start eating?
RICHARD. Taste it first, as you usually do.
KEEPER. My lord, I don’t dare. Sir Pierce of Exton, who just came from the King, orders the opposite.
RICHARD. The devil take Henry of Lancaster, and you too! My patience is worn out, and I’m tired of it.
[He hits the Keeper.]
KEEPER. Help, help, help!
[Exton and armed Servants enter.]
RICHARD. What’s this? What does death mean by this violent attack? Villain, your own hand gives me the weapon for your death.
[He grabs a weapon and kills one of them.]
You go and fill another room in hell.
[He kills another, then Exton strikes him down.]

The hand that knocks me down like this will burn in a fire that never goes out. Exton, your savage hand has stained the King’s own land with the King’s blood. Rise, rise, my soul! Your place is up on high, while my heavy flesh sinks down here to die.
[He dies.]

EXTON. As full of courage as he was of royal blood! I have spilled both. Oh, I wish this deed were good! Now the devil who told me I did well says this deed is written down in hell. I’ll carry this dead king to the living king. Take the rest away, and bury them here.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 6 — Windsor. An Apartment in the Castle
paragraphs: [Trumpets play. King Henry and York enter with Lords and Attendants.]
KING HENRY. Kind uncle York, the latest news we’ve heard is that the rebels have burned our town of Cirencester in Gloucestershire. But we haven’t heard whether they’ve been captured or killed.
[Northumberland enters.]
Welcome, my lord. What’s the news?

NORTHUMBERLAND. First, I wish all happiness to your sacred majesty. The next news is this: I have sent to London the heads of Salisbury, Spencer, Blunt and Kent. How they were captured is described in full in this paper here.
KING HENRY. We thank you for your efforts, noble Percy, and we will add well-earned rewards to your merit.
[Fitzwater enters.]
FITZWATER. My lord, I have sent from Oxford to London the heads of Brocas and Sir Bennet Seely. They were two of the dangerous conspiring traitors who plotted your terrible overthrow at Oxford.
KING HENRY. Your efforts won’t be forgotten, Fitzwater. Your merit is truly noble, I know that well.
[Harry Percy enters with the Bishop of Carlisle.]

PERCY. The chief conspirator, the Abbot of Westminster, weighed down by a guilty conscience and bitter depression, has given up his body to the grave. But here is Carlisle, still alive, to receive your royal judgment and the sentence for his arrogance.

KING HENRY. Carlisle, this is your sentence. Choose some secluded place, some religious house, better than the one you have now, and enjoy your life there. As long as you live in peace, you’ll die free of trouble. Though you have always been my enemy, I have seen bright sparks of honor in you.
[Exton enters with attendants carrying a coffin.]
EXTON. Great king, in this coffin I present your buried fear. Here lies, without breath, the mightiest of your greatest enemies, Richard of Bordeaux, whom I have brought here.
KING HENRY. Exton, I don’t thank you. With your deadly hand you have done a deed that will bring disgrace on my head and on this whole famous country.
EXTON. My lord, I did this deed because of words from your own mouth.

KING HENRY. People who need poison don’t love it, and I don’t love you. Though I wished him dead, I hate the murderer and love the murdered man. Take a guilty conscience as payment for your work, but not my good word or my royal favor. Go wander with Cain through the darkness of night, and never show your face by day or in the light. Lords, I declare my soul is full of sorrow that blood had to be spattered on me to make me grow. Come, mourn with me for what I grieve over, and put on gloomy black at once. I’ll make a journey to the Holy Land to wash this blood off my guilty hand. Walk solemnly after me, and honor my mourning here by weeping behind this coffin of a man who died too soon.
[They exit.]
